#3632. GTA 6 Buying Guide: Get Ready For Sticker Shock

Rockstar's GTA 6 finally releases on November 19, and if you're looking to play the game, you'll also need a console--and those are more expensive than ever. Here's a quick buying guide to help you understand what you need and how much the items will cost. 

A console

First, you'll need a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S console. The least expensive option for buying a new system outright is the Xbox Series S, which costs $500. Unfortunately, that's $200 more expensive than the system cost at launch in 2020--there are a number macroeconomic and AI factors that drove prices up significantly.

A new Xbox Series X, meanwhile, costs $750 for a system with no disc drive, or $800 for a console with a disc drive. GTA 6 is not available on a disc, but having a disc drive may still be important to you for other games and media like DVDs and Blu-rays. 

Switching to PlayStation, the least expensive system on Sony's side is the $600 digital edition, scaling up to $900 for a PS5 Pro (with a disc drive). PS5 Pro, as the most powerful of these options, is likely to provide the best experience from a technical and graphical standpoint, although the gameplay itself should be identical across all platforms.

These are all prices for brand-new units, but Sony offers certified refurbished PS5 consoles starting at $500. A certified refurbished Xbox Series S, meanwhile, goes for $400. These are the prices from Sony and Microsoft directly, but you can find secondhand consoles at a variety of other retailers, along with places like eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and Craigslist. As usual, check your local or preferred retailer to see the latest prices.

New and certified refurbished consoles come with everything you need--including the system, controller, and power cords. You will need a TV or monitor, but the odds are good that if you're looking to play GTA 6, you probably already have one. 

People on platforms outside PlayStation and Xbox are out of luck, as GTA 6 has not been announced for Switch 2 or PC. A PC edition is expected to release in early 2027, but there is no word on a Switch 2 version. 

The game

To play GTA 6 you will need to buy GTA 6. The game's standard edition goes for $80, with its Ultimate Edition selling for $100. As mentioned, the game is not available on a disc. That being said, retailers are selling the $80 edition in stores, though you only get a code in the box. The $100 edition appears to be exclusive to digital storefronts.

The $100 Ultimate Edition includes loads of extras, including a variety of cosmetics and even in-game shops that people who buy the $80 edition cannot access. Since GTA 6 is a digital-exclusive game, there is no reason to worry about units selling out, but if you do want to preorder, you get the Vintage Vice City Pack and a free month of GTA+.

GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013--adjusted for inflation, that's about $85 today.

You will also need an internet connection to install GTA 6, since it's a digital only game. It's a beefy one, too, weighing in at a reported 201GB. Thankfully, preloading begins on November 12, a full week before the game launches. That means you'll be able to begin downloading it early in the hopes of being ready to go on November 19.

November 12 is also when GTA 6's code-in-a-box copies will be available to buy at physical stores. You're not getting a week of early access, though, as the game does not unlock fully until November 19.

Do you need PS Plus or Game Pass?

GTA 6 is a strictly single-player game, and as such, you likely will not need PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass to play. Rockstar has yet to confirm this, however. 

Rockstar is surely going to release a new version of GTA Online at some point--some believe that will happen in early 2027. And at that point, you'll likely need a membership. But for launch, there is no online or multiplayer support, so we don't think a subscription to PS Plus or Game Pass would be required. 

Why no disc?

Neither Rockstar nor studio owner Take-Two have provided a reason for GTA 6 being a digital exclusive, but the answer seems pretty obvious: It's all about money. Rockstar makes more money from digital game sales, and having no disc eliminates the secondhand market. 

“A disc can be resold or rented a hundred times, and Rockstar earns nothing after that first sale," Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics said. 

The code-in-a-box strategy for physical games has been around for a long time already, and while people might complain online about the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6, the game is going to sell phenomenally no matter what, Mat Piscatella of Circana says.

Beyond these factors, consumer spending patterns have trended increasingly toward digital since the early 2010s. GTA 6 is such a large game in terms of its file size, so making it digital-exclusive also saves Rockstar and Take-Two money by not needing to print a second disc, if one was ever needed.

Full House might not be hailed as one of the best sitcoms of all time by many, but I have always been a massive fan of the show. I used to watch it every night on Nick at Nite and even own the entire series on DVD. I’ve always adored the Tanners and their extended family and can’t imagine any of them being played by any other actors; but it turns out that Lori Loughlin almost didn’t get to play Aunt Becky.

A majority of the Full House cast reunited at ‘90s Con in Connecticut and appeared on a panel discussing the show. During the panel, John Stamos shared his experience with the show’s creator, Jeff Franklin, when it came to casting Aunt Becky, aka his eventual long-term love interest on the show.

Lori came on at first, and I was like — I think we did some readings together before. I told [series creator] Jeff [Franklin], ‘I don’t know. She’s cute, and she’s adorable. I don’t think she’s tough enough to put Jesse in his place.’

Good casting can make or break a project, especially when it comes to the chemistry between two actors who are playing characters that are romantically linked. At the time, Full House wasn’t considered a hit by any means, so it makes sense that Stamos would want to get the casting right to ensure the show would continue.

While Stamos’ Uncle Jesse and Lori Loughlin’s Aunt Becky eventually became the best couple on the show, their relationship wasn’t always a walk in the park. Jesse was instantly smitten with Becky, as he was with most women on the show, but the same was not true for her character. Thus, it was important that Loughlin be able to play off Stamos’s character in order to build up that will-they, won’t-they tension.

Thankfully, the show’s creator didn’t listen to Stamos and did go on to cast Loughlin in the role. In turn, the When Calls the Heart actress proved Stamos wrong and put him and his character in his place on the first day of set.

Scene one, she came and she put me in my place fast. She had the perfect combination of this adorable, sweet girl. But, when it was time for me to get in trouble, you had no problem [playing] that out.

For those who don’t remember, Jesse meets Becky at the Tanner house and instantly tries to hit on her. Unlike most of the women who swoon at his feet, Becky challenged Jesse’s flirting attempts and even compared him to her baby brother, which gutted him. However, despite Becky’s apprehensions, she did end up falling for Jesse’s charm, and the two got together (for the first time) during the second season’s Christmas episode.

Hiring Loughlin turned out to be one of the best decisions, and the show steadily started to grow its fan base. It’s wild to think that she was initially only hired for six episodes and went on to become a fan favorite character. It turns out Aunt Becky was the missing piece all along.

#3630. Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers

Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game sold 10 million copies over its first three days. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, meanwhile, sold 10 million copies in three days as well.

If you’re looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items.

“S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired combat puts you in the middle of a Chinese action movie,” Richard Wakeling wrote in GameSpot’s Phantom Blade Zero review.

#3629. Inside Airbnb.org’s Gala With Jimmy Kimmel, Charli xcx, and Brian Chesky

Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.

“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”

Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.

And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

#3628. These Sony Over-Ear Headphones Are Just $88 Right Now

Not everybody needs, wants, or can afford the "best" headphones available, especially when they can easily cost half a grand. If the $450+ Sony XM6s, which I called the best over-ear headphones of 2025 (and 2026 so far), are not in your budget, then perhaps the more affordable Sony WH-CH720Ns could be. While they're not quite as premium, they're significantly cheaper and offer good enough audio quality for most people.

Right now, you can get them for $88 (originally $179.99) on Amazon, their second-lowest price ever according to price tracking tools. Thopugh they've dropped below $100 before, all three colorways have not been available at their current price at the same time until now.

These are Sony's entry-level over-ear headphones, and the company mostly made cuts in the design and build. When you hold them, they might feel hollow and light, but they're still comfortable since the earcups are well-cushioned, as noted in CNET's review. However, Sony did not make as many sacrifices in the audio or ANC department, which, at the end of the day, is what's most important.

These headphones use the same Sony Sound Connect app as the flagship models and share some of the same features, like multipoint technology to connect to up to two devices. They also come with Google Fast Pair and Find My Device support, nice features to have for convenience, especially if you misplace them. You can get 35 hours of battery life with ANC on and 50 hours with ANC off, and the charging is quick, with three minutes giving you three hours of juice.

The ANC is not as good as the latest XM6, but it works great for under $100, according to Mashable's review, and it will block most ambient noise outdoors or indoors. Transparency mode is also great, allowing you to have conversations and hear bikes or cars passing by. The adjustable EQ in the app means you can tweak the crisp and vibrant sound of the WH-CH720N to your liking.

The “Unlocked With Savannah Chrisley” host stunned fans on Tuesday, October 27, by revealing that she was pregnant. While she initially kept her partner’s identity private, Us exclusively identified Galanis as the man Savannah routinely referred to as just “J” or “Jason” on her podcast.

Marriage records obtained by People subsequently confirmed that Galanis, 56, and Savannah quietly tied the knot at the Cayman Islands Baptist Church in July after one year of dating.

“We ended up getting married in the Cayman Islands in July,” Savannah later reiterated on the “Golden Ticket” podcast on Sunday, November 1. “We did everything there, but we haven’t filed it here [in the U.S.] — or else then it would be public record.”

Inside the NBA fans were hit with some major news last week, as longtime co-host Ernie Johnson confirmed his plan to leave the show at the end of the professional basketball season. Right now, many are simply taking the time to pay tribute to the man affectionately known as “E.J.” However, there are those who are also questioning what lies ahead for the show in the long run without Johnson. The man himself recently expressed his hope that the show will go on, and there’s also been an update on ESPN’s alleged feelings about that.

To put it mildly, Johnson is one of the mainstays of Inside, given he’s been hosting the show for 37 years now. 70-year-old Johnson announced his intention to exit the show nearly a week ago in a social media video that’s since gone viral. The veteran sports journalist confirmed that he wasn’t retiring from broadcasting entirely, though. He’ll continue to serve as a March Madness analyst and produce content under his 32 Bowties production company. Nevertheless, he’s stepping down from Inside as a way to “slow down a bit.”

Johnson recently caught up with Front Office Sports Tonight to discuss his big decision and plans for the future. When addressing what may lie ahead for his long-running basketball talk show, Johnson expressed optimism:

I don’t want to be blamed for ending Inside the NBA. I’m stepping away from my role on there. I would hope that they could continue the show in some form. And there are plenty of great studio hosts out there who could do what I do.

On paper, it would definitely make sense to keep the TNT-turned-ESPN sports show on the air, considering its popularity. It’s still hard not to wonder, however, how viewership may be affected by Ernie Johnson’s absence next season. Plus, there’s the fact that Charles Barkley has been discussing retirement again as well. With that, sources are now saying that ESPN has been giving the future some thought amid these developments.

Shaq Explains Why Inside The NBA Works, But I’m Just Loving The Ernie Johnson Detail He Revealed

Weeks before Johnson confirmed his intention to leave Inside, Barkley already indicated that his longtime co-star would do just that. The “Round Mound of Rebound” also said at the time that he was planning to exit the show after this current season as well due to him and Johnson being a “package deal.” Considering that Johnson and Barkley have shared the screen for over 25 years, their dual exits would mark a major shift. However, per FOS’ sources, ESPN remains committed to keeping the show going even without the pair.

That would theoretically leave co-hosts Kenny Smith and Shaquille O’Neal alongside two others. Interestingly, since Johnson shared his news, Barkley hasn’t said anything more about whether he’ll ride off into the sunset as well. Johnson was also asked about Barkley’s plans when he appeared on FOS Tonight, and he had this to say about him:

As for what Chuck is going to do, I have learned many many moons ago, you never try to predict what the Chuckster is going to do. But he and I have had a lot of conversations in the past about what we’re going to do, so I will leave that final word to him.

If any other Inside the NBA fans are like me, they’ll be waiting with bated breath for Charles Barkley to deliver a definitive decision. The fact that Ernie Johnson is leaving (for some well-deserved time with his loved ones) is already tough to think about, so Barkley’s exit would also be a lot. At the very least, though, it’s encouraging that ESPN is reportedly still aiming to keep the show on the air for the foreseeable future.

Check out Inside the NBA’s next broadcast, which will hit ESPN on Wednesday, November 4, with NBA Tip Off starting at 6 p.m. ET amid the 2026 TV schedule.

“I am living in a nightmare I can’t wake up from. My husband has been having an affair. I have been fed lie after lie after lie for months. I am tired of lies,” she wrote at the time.

Hila shared that she “could sense something was wrong” in her marriage and “tried to ask [Ethan] questions and share my concerns and hurt feelings,” but “I was met with dismissive answers and no action. Hila said she and Ethan were separated and that she was focused on “taking care of myself and my children, one day at a time.”

#3623. Actor Keith McDermott on Robert Wilson’s Legacy and Ghostwriting His Memoir: “I Saw a Robert Wilson Play and It Changed My Life”

Over the more than 50-year period of his career, Wilson was arguably the most produced American theater director in Europe, if not the world. His aesthetic style has permeated European theater and opera culture to the extent that few directors have remained uninfluenced by what is commonly referred to as the “Wilsonian” use of lighting, set design, and performance style. However, he is not well-known in his own country.

The Robert Wilson productions that have reached the United States are some of the most iconic stage works of the 20th and 21st century: Einstein on the Beach and Lohengrin at the Metropolitan Opera House and at least 10 full productions at Brooklyn Academy of Music. Even in New York, Wilson’s artistic home, and even among artists, a not uncommon response at the mention of his name is “Should I know who that is?”

However, there is another response from New Yorkers of my generation, those of us living here when the city was at the artistic peak of the ’60s and ’70s, when Balanchine oversaw the New York City Ballet, Joe Papp headed the Public Theater, Andy Warhol ran The Factory, and apartments were affordable. That response, my response, is “I saw a Robert Wilson play and it changed my life.”

In 1975, a friend offered me a free ticket to a Broadway play. The title was A Letter for Queen Victoria, and I assumed I was in for a fusty historical drama, but as a young actor pursuing a commercial career, I never passed up an opportunity to see a play, especially if it was free.

Robert Wilson's A Letter for Queen Victoria.

The play began before the houselights went down as a young man and woman in ordinary dress stood in front of the curtain on opposite sides of the stage slowly turning in place. Nothing about their slow, hypnotic movement suggested “performance” until the houselights began to dim. Still turning, they raised their hands from their sides. Their palms, pressed in turmeric, became a blur of orange as their revolutions increased in speed and the curtain rose. The cast included the director’s grandmother as Queen Victoria, and a neurodivergent teenager, Christopher Knowles, whose nonacting presence broke the fourth wall, as he shielded his eyes from the stage lights to gaze into the house.

Audience members left in droves. A woman shouted something about child abuse on her way to the exit. But I sat mesmerized as the play evolved through a series of scenes unconnected by narrative or plot, fantastic in design, exquisitely lit, and often extraordinarily slow. Those of us who stayed until the end leapt to our feet, applauding and cheering for the actors, call after call. I stumbled from the theater into the city night feeling as if I had fallen in love.

My enthusiasm for that play led to both a professional and personal involvement with Bob (as anyone who knows him calls him). As a performer, I have appeared in five Wilson productions in various parts of the world and understudied him in a one‐man show. As a writer, I published an article about his chair collection and a roman à clef in which a character based on Bob pretty much takes over the book. In addition to our working relationship, Bob, a fellow Texan, has been my friend for over 50 years, and early in 2023 he asked me to ghostwrite his memoir.

Our sessions began formally at the Watermill Center, “a laboratory for the arts and humanities” on the South Fork of Long Island, founded by Bob in 1992. He had an apartment there where he stayed when he was in town. Assuming we’d work through his life chronologically, I came armed with questions about his childhood in Waco, Texas, his parents, and his schooling. But later, transcribing our recorded sessions, I cringed at my attempts to get Bob back on topic as he segued into a tale about absentmindedly depositing his airline ticket into a mailbox, then trying to board the plane with the postcards he had meant to mail, or a harrowing memory of six weeks spent in a Greek prison for a bit of hash discovered by airport security. My interruptions only spoiled the spontaneous flow of Bob’s thoughts.

Bob was a storyteller. Everyone who knew and worked with him was familiar with his stories, often told in a regional Texas twang and often more than once – and occasionally with a remarkable addendum. For instance, I knew that in his 20s, while working as a recreational therapist at the Goldwater Memorial Hospital for the terminally ill, Bob had choreographed a “dance” for quadriplegic patients in iron lungs, tying Day-Glo strings to mouth sticks they used to turn book pages that connected to mobiles hung from the ceiling. But in the retelling, I learned that Bob, after attending an Otis Redding concert, had persuaded the singer to come to the ward to accompany his quadriplegic dancers.

Once we gave up the chronological approach and Bob, unburdened by the need to deliver “The Story of My Life,” began to think in terms of “Life Stories,” our process relaxed and stories flowed. In addition to scheduled sessions, I could collect them everywhere, because Bob told them everywhere: at dinner parties, in the car, over the coffee and English muffins I began to deliver early each morning, or on our daily golf cart trips around the Watermill grounds. I always met him armed with my tape recorder.

A story he told frequently, both publicly, in interviews, and privately, was about seeing a policeman about to strike a young boy and intervening. From the sounds the boy made, Bob realized he was deaf. The boy, Raymond Andrews, was diagnosed as ineducable, but Bob realized he simply relied on visual cues not words. At 27 Bob became Raymond’s legal guardian and enrolled him in a school for the deaf. Raymond flourished in the creative community Bob created at his Spring Street loft (in SoHo before it was SoHo). Using Raymond’s drawings and his own observations of the boy, Bob created Deafman Glance, a seven-hour silent opera that signaled his European renown.

Bob told many stories about Jessye Norman, but the one that always brought him and his listeners to tears was of the great singer attempting to get through a Winterreise concert just after 9/11. During the third song, Norman began to cry and had to stop singing. When she regained control, she stood for 10 minutes, motionless, in silence, while the audience wept.

Bob’s vast social network also included socialites and celebrities, and those stories are filled with irresistible gossip: Marlene Dietrich divulged the name of the only contemporary American performer she completely admired (spoiler alert: it was Tina Turner); Diana Vreeland swallowed vials of cod liver oil to act as a buffer for vodka before an evening out; Samuel Beckett claimed that his lead actress in Happy Days was so brilliant because she didn’t understand a word she said.

In June of 2025, Bob went to Lithuania to stage rehearsals of a new production and then to Ljubljana, Slovenia, to direct Tristan and Isolde. When he was away, he sent me emails with story topics for our next session: “Ask me about my boat trip in the Middle East with Helen de Rothschild,” “Ask me about Louis Malle offering me the lead in Pretty Baby.”

When Bob returned to Watermill in July, we were to meet for final interviews, although by that time, I had all the material needed for the book. Shortly before my travels, I received a message that Bob’s health had declined, and he would be unable to see me. He died a week later on July 31 in his Watermill apartment.

Months after Bob’s death, I was still listening to and transcribing our taped conversations. In one conversation, recorded when we were having dinner at an Indian restaurant, Bob was telling me a story about being dressed as Santa Claus and handing out presents in Bali, where he spent every Christmas. Suddenly, he stopped mid-sentence and after a short silence, said, “I love you, Keith.”

I love you too, Bob, you changed my life.

THE SPACE BEHIND THE FACE, a memoir by the visionary theater director and visual artist, Robert Wilson, is published by Penguin Press and arrives on November 3.

#3620. Former Xbox Exec Shares Her Side Of The Story After Mysterious Depature

Helen Chiang, the veteran Xbox staffer who got promoted in July and left the company amid mysterious circumstances just recently, has shared her side of the story--but her response doesn't close the book on this saga.

In a LinkedIn post titled "Clarity is Kindess," which itself is a reference to her former boss (and Xbox CEO) Asha Sharma's much-ridiculed and cringey mantra, said it's "not accurate" that she was "fired for a policy violation" as multiple reports said.

Chiang said she will not "turn this into a play-by-play" and reveal the specifics, but she wanted to speak out to dispel rumors. "What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize."

She went on to "set the record straight" by claiming she did not leak confidential company information to the press as some had speculated. "I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job," she said, adding that this includes having no contact with any journalist who reached out to her before today to ask for her side of the story.

Chiang went on to say she did not leave Xbox to join a competitor. "You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build," she said

"Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here," she said.  

That may all be true, but it's also unquestionable that people regularly spend lengthy periods of their career at one company, in high-level positions, and then move to other companies.

Third, Chiang said she "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity."

"I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record," she said.

Chiang added that she did not leave Xbox because she was "passed over for a bigger role." She said that since having children, she became more "intentional about how I define ambition and success." She said she has purposefully not sought out bigger roles or jobs with more responsibilities; she said she hadn't interviewed for a job since 2011.

"My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact," she said, adding that she did not ask to become Xbox's first-ever COO.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.

#3618. Spanish Soccer Player Jesus De Miguel Dead at 30 After On-Field Collision

Spanish soccer player Jesús de Miguel has died at age 30 after an on-field collision.

The CD Tenerife striker died early Tuesday, November 3, after reportedly being struck in the chest by another player during a game against FC Andorra on Monday, November 2.

“Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00 a.m., of Jesús de Miguel Alameda,” the soccer team said in a statement written in Spanish on Tuesday.

“There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness. We stand alongside his devastated family, alongside his loved ones, alongside all of tinerfeñismo that today weeps for this cruel outcome,” CD Tenerife continued.

According to the BBC and The Guardian, de Miguel suffered head and chest injuries after colliding with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during the final minutes of Monday’s game at Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz, Spain. He reportedly suffered a cardiac arrest.

Monday’s game between Tenerife and Andorra was abandoned, per the BBC. The score had been 2-2.

CD Tenerife said Monday evening that de Miguel was taken to the Nuestra Señora de Candelaria University Hospital and was in “stable but serious” condition. In an update later on Monday, the team said de Miguel’s condition had “worsened neurologically.”

On Tuesday, opposing team FC Andorra paid tribute to de Miguel in an Instagram post, as did other Spanish teams.

“There are no words to express the sadness of a loss like this,” the team said. “From FC Andorra we want to transfer our deepest condolences to the family, friends and colleagues of Jesús de Miguel, as well as the entire family of CD Tenerife.”

FC Andorra’s post continued, “We are with you in these very difficult times. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

Fellow Spanish team FC Barcelona shared via X on Tuesday, “From FC Barcelona, we deeply regret the tragic news of the passing of Jesús de Miguel, CD Tenerife player. Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times.”

Real Madrid said in a statement, “Real Madrid C. F., its president, and its Board of Directors deeply regret the passing of Jesús de Miguel, player of C. D. Tenerife. Real Madrid wishes to express its condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones.”

The Madrid side held a moment of silence in de Miguel’s honor before its training session Tuesday.

“Before starting the training session at Ciudad Real Madrid, the players and coaching staff of Real Madrid observed a minute of silence for the passing of Jesús de Miguel, a player from C.D. Tenerife,” the club said in a statement.

Star Trek: The Next Generation's Brent Spiner revealed he had a small part to play in Patrick Stewart's famous time hosting Saturday Night Live. A story about the Data actor's attempt to get on the show is making rounds after his co-star's death, and I absolutely love it.

Spiner's story popped up in a special video from Dropping Names With Brent And Jonny, which compiled each time the hosts talked about their former co-star and friend, Stewart. This led to a hilarious story in which Spiner tried to get on SNL, only for them to inquire about Stewart instead:

My now-wife, she was a publicist on [TNG], and when she became a publicist she said, 'Is there anything you would like to do? I'll see if I can get that for you.' I said, 'Yeah, I want to host Saturday Night Live.' She said, 'Ok,' and she called them and she said, 'Well, I called them and they said we'd like to have Patrick Stewart.'

Brent Spiner may be the funniest person in Star Trek, which is evident enough from stories from co-stars and the Generations movie. That was enough to get him on Night Court, but Saturday Night Live is reserved for the leads. As such, their staff wanted Patrick Stewart, and as we know, Stewart is who they got.

As A Star Trek Fan I'm Eternally Grateful For What Patrick Stewart Did For The Franchise

Patrick Stewart only hosted SNL once in the 90s, but the night lives on in the show's history thanks to a story John Mulaney worked into his stand-up comedy. Mulaney stressed that Stewart's delivery when introducing Salt-N-Pepa was interesting because he sounded surprised by the Pepa bit of it, though people debate whether it really was that silly after watching the clip.

As for other stand-out moments of the Saturday Night Live appearance, there are a few skits that stand out. There's a skit I love that combined Star Trek: The Next Generation with The Love Boat, as well as another about him working in an erotic bakery shop. Both had me laughing out loud when I watched, so those who can seek it out certainly should.

It's yet another story about Stewart appearing on another show, which I found just after writing about Jeremy Clarkson having him on the set of Top Gear. I'll always appreciate the wild Star Trek stories about Stewart, but I've heard a good deal of them already. Learning his experience on other shows is great, and further illustrates what kind of man he was behind the scenes.

Both his Star Trek and Marvel co-stars insist that Patrick Stewart was exceptionally kind. He played a Captain on television and a super-powered Professor in the X-Men, and by all accounts, both were a good show of just how heroic he was as a real-life individual. As a fan, it's great to see the man measured up to all I imagined he'd be.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family of Patrick Stewart, and the friends who continue to mourn him. It's been great to see all the stories hitting the internet, and how it's given fans comfort in the wake of a tremendous loss to the Star Trek world.

#3616. Is Ken Paxton’s Senate Campaign in Texas the Bitter End of Trumpism?

At Coyote Crossing Saloon, a smoke-filled dive bar off Interstate 37, a 64-year-old Texas native named Tracey was showing me his teeth. He’s missing about half of them—a casualty, he said, of toothpicks soaked in horse liniment that serve as a potent stimulant for truckers looking to stay up late on long-haul drives. Tracey is a big fan of President Donald Trump. He voted for him three times and still supports him, even after all the excesses of his second term. But he can’t stomach Ken Paxton.

Dragging on a cigarette, he pointed to the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate’s alleged corruption, his reputed infidelity, and the case of a plea deal his office offered to a Waco man charged with sexually abusing a young boy. “Just because you have all this money, how are you gonna just do as you please and nobody’s gonna say nothing?” Tracey remains a fan of the state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott. “He’ll win, so I’m happy about that.” But Paxton? “Get him out of there.”

Texas attorney general Ken Paxton embarked on a bus tour of the Lone Star State as his Senate campaign draws to a close.

If Paxton has lost voters like Tracey, Republicans might be in trouble. Texas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and this seat could determine who will control Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Yet the collapse of Trump’s approval across the country has put even red states like Texas in play for Democrats, creating a powerful undercurrent that Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, has surfed to a narrow but steady lead in the polls. That’s turned Texas into a money pit: $500 million has been blown on advertising already, thanks in part to at least $168 million pumped into the state by Elon Musk, and it’s on track to be the most expensive Senate race in history.

It didn’t have to be this difficult. Since 2002, the seat has been occupied by Senator John Cornyn, who ran for reelection with the backing of the Republican establishment and a sizable war chest. But in the primary, the president backed Paxton, a scandal-plagued culture warrior who went above and beyond Trump’s loyalty tests, while Cornyn drew suspicion that he was fair-weather MAGA. Now Trump has placed a risky bet. These midterms are a referendum on the president, but this race, more than any other, is a gauge of his movement: Can a candidate with many of Trump’s failings but little of his charisma careen into the United States Senate?

Even in the ruby-red counties of West Texas, Trump’s support is slipping. Will Paxton pay for it?

A crowd in Sherman, Texas, settles down into movie theater recliners to watch Paxton speak.

This is the final sprint of the Paxton campaign, a frenetic bus odyssey dubbed the Come and Take It Tour. (There’s a cannon printed on the side of the bus.) The voyage has swept through the border towns of McAllen and Laredo, up through exurbs like Selma—just outside San Antonio—on to Austin and Waco and Dallas, then out through hundreds of miles of high plains to the West Texas towns of Amarillo and Lubbock, and then down to Corpus Christi for a rally with Trump himself.

“The person that is without sin, please cast the first stone,” said Pastor Ruben Mendez in his opening prayer at Paxton’s campaign event in Selma. The room was silent. “I don’t think so. I don’t think there’s anybody that can do that.” Mendez, the pastor of Iglesia Shalom, a small nondenominational church tucked down an alleyway in a suburb nearby, was speaking to a crowd crammed into the Blue Bonnet Palace, a country music venue in a corrugated iron barn just off the highway. A cardboard cutout of Brooks & Dunn hung above the stage alongside a motionless disco ball.

Paxton is locked in a close race with James Talarico, whom Trump has nicknamed “Talafreako.”

The pastor’s reminder that “King David was a flawed man” was met with scattered applause. If the subtext of this homily wasn’t clear enough, a protester soon made it explicit. “Why were you in Dubai?” a young man yelled as Paxton took the stage. He was swiftly bounced by security to chants of “USA!” from the faithful.

The protester was referencing the latest chapter of the biblical Paxton oppo file. The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve 2024 partying in Dubai with Tracy Duhon, his rumored mistress, as well as two men who were then fugitives from US justice, one of whom had donated to Paxton. This indiscretion joins a long list of scandals that supporters of Paxton are willing to overlook to back the candidate (and, perhaps more importantly, keep Texas red). On the tour, they often invoked faith to make their case.

House Republican Darrell Issa, who served as chairman of the House Oversight Committee and worked with Paxton when he was a crusading state attorney general, stumped for the candidate on his swing from San Antonio to Georgetown. When I asked why he felt compelled to campaign for Paxton given the baggage, Issa echoed Pastor Mendez.

The line was lengthy to get into the rally in Corpus Christi.

“Is President Trump a man without flaws? No. But neither was Andy Jackson, neither was Bill Clinton, neither was Abraham Lincoln,” the congressman said. “So you judge somebody in elected office based on the honor that they bring to the office, the energy they bring, and the initiatives that they’re involved in, and that’s where [Paxton] excels. So am I going to say that this is somebody that, like our savior, was without sin? No. But I’m not somebody without sin, and neither are any of the voters.”

Some would argue that Paxton’s sins are more exotic than those of your ordinary Texan. He was charged with two counts of felony securities fraud by Texas prosecutors and in 2024 reached a deal to avoid trial that involved paying nearly $300,000 in restitution. Separately, the Texas House impeached him in 2023 on charges of bribery, corruption, and abusing his office. (Paxton has denied the allegations that led to his impeachment.) With state legislators under intense pressure from Trump, he was acquitted by the Senate. “Yes, it is true that my intervention through TRUTH SOCIAL saved Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from going down,” Trump boasted afterward.

There’s also Paxton’s reputation for jet-setting: In his 11 years as attorney general, an Associated Press investigation found, Paxton spent an extraordinary amount of time traveling to plush locales including “California wine country, Caribbean resorts, and European tourism hot spots.” It cost the taxpayers at least $1.9 million to cover the expenses of his security detail. And then there was, of course, the 2013 surveillance video that caught Paxton pocketing a man’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (His campaign called the incident a “mix-up,” and Paxton returned the pen after he was contacted by a sheriff’s deputy.)

Even some of the ads supporting him carry a bit of a shrug. Angela Paxton, who is suing her husband for divorce on “biblical grounds,” which is King James for “cheating,” appears in a spot urging Texans to vote Republican down the ticket. “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room,” she says at the start of the ad, which ends without any further mention of the elephant.

For many in the Republican establishment, these indiscretions have pushed Paxton beyond the pale, but that’s of little concern to the nominee’s supporters. “He may not have his life together,” said Janet, a Paxton backer from Corpus Christi, “but he’s better than the alternative.”

There was strong turnout for a Trump rally to support Paxton in Corpus Christi.

Kevin, a 62-year-old from the San Antonio suburbs, brought his wife to see Paxton speak in Selma. “I believe in this country there is a battle between good and evil,” he said. “I try to judge characters in a biblical sense.” Where does that leave Paxton, a man accused of violating quite a few of the commandments? “I’m okay with Ken Paxton,” Kevin said, waving a hand as I ran down the list of transgressions. “I believe Trump is the best president we’ve ever had. And we got to have people in there to support him.”

Jason Norton, 50, a bearded and tattooed pastor at King’s Trail Cowboy Church who delivered the prayer at Paxton’s stop north of Dallas, had a similarly permissive view of his alleged infidelity. “Christian does not mean perfect. Nobody would approve of that. And I’m sure he probably regrets it. But what he did hurt himself and his family. What Talarico’s doing will hurt the entire state.”

In a quaint historic town north of Fort Worth, I met Steve Bannon at the Texas headquarters of his War Room podcast. A longtime Paxton backer, Bannon has spent much of this campaign season in the state, broadcasting to the Trump base while helping to advise the Republican’s campaign. “We have not seen the data yet that shows part of our coalition actually coming out and voting against Trump,” Bannon told me. “I think most of them are staying home. That’s a huge win for us. If they come out and vote against us, we’re fucked.”

After Musk dumped $168 million into the race, Republican super PACs pumped out ads casting Talarico as too extreme for Texas. The Democrat’s disposition as a love-thy-trans-neighbor seminarian is a cover for something far more sinister, the argument goes. “Even the Bible says the devil comes as an angel of light,” Pastor Norton told me. “Just because somebody’s sweet doesn’t mean they’re right.”

It doesn’t help the Democrat that, like many in the party, he dabbled in the kind of heady progressive rhetoric trendy in the early 2020s, something anathema to red-state voters. Among the hits, of which Texans are regularly reminded in Paxton’s speeches, Trump’s posts, and endless campaign ads: Talarico’s remark in 2021 that “God is nonbinary”; his comment in the same year that there are “six really common biological sexes” and his description of himself as “a Christian who hates Christianity”; his 2022 run for reelection to the Texas House, which he said would be a vegan campaign, reasoning that reducing meat consumption was “necessary to fight climate change”; and his comment that the American flag is a “complicated symbol.”

Talarico has since walked back some of these lines, calling them “cringey” and “provocative.” But Musk’s money cannon ensures Texas voters are relentlessly confronted by them, and the race appears to have tightened in the final stretch of the campaign. For voters susceptible to these kinds of criticisms of Talarico, a Paxton rally provides a potent narrative. The notes from his stump speech that draw the loudest applause can drive the neutral observer to mild psychosis. We’re going to stop Sharia law from coming to Texas, goes one. The Pfizer vaccine was less than 1% effective, offers another. And of course: James Talarico wants to trans your kids.

Paxton was greeted by a sea of red hats as he arrived onstage.

That last bit is one of Paxton’s favorites, and it hit hard in some of the more incandescent-red counties we passed through. “I mean, this guy is really obsessed with transitions,” Paxton mused into the mic, winding up for the big delivery. “He wants to transition our kids, he wants to transition Texas off of the oil and gas industry.” (Wry pause.) “How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas!” (Applause, cheers, hoots, and hollers as Paxton stepped back from the podium and smirked, almost bashfully, eyes darting back and forth as he soaked up the response.)

Some of the attacks on Talarico are more extreme. Paxton and a number of his campaign surrogates warned that the Democrat would help usher Sharia law into Texas. When I met with Bannon, he introduced me to Patriot Mobile cofounder Glenn Story, who’s active in Texas politics and counts Paxton as a friend. “I’m the one who told him to start talking about Sharia law,” Story said. “You go up to the Costco near me? Towelheads everywhere,” he said, using a slur for Muslims. “Come with me, I’ll show you.” Reluctant to spend my afternoon driving around looking for people who might appear Muslim, I declined.

At a stop in Sanger, a small town in a ruby-red county north of Dallas, the star of the warm-up acts was Brandon Gill, a young House Republican who has emerged as a favorite among the party’s hard-line base. He walked out to a roaring welcome, and one man shouted, “Brandon for president!” The heckle was deftly parried by Gill: “Let’s say Ken Paxton for Senate first.” As Gill ran through the list of well-worn criticisms of Talarico’s liberalism, Stacey, a woman in the crowd, shouted: “It’s demonic!”

“That’s right,” Gill replied. “It is demonic.”

Outside the venue, I spoke with Stacey and her friend Claire, two Paxton superfans from nearby who called themselves “MAHA moms.”

“He seems like a nice man,” Stacey said of Talarico. “He’s just misguided. If he was my neighbor, I’d vote for him to be on my HOA board. But not for the Senate.” They were confident that Paxton would keep the seat red. But Claire was concerned that her parents, both Republicans, had written in names in protest of Paxton’s candidacy.

On a good day, Ken Paxton is not a gifted orator. This was a bad day. It was Sunday night, the last stop of the weekend, and the candidate walked onto a stage at Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille in Sherman, a highway town 60 miles north of Dallas, to speak to a few dozen supporters picking at tacos while leaning back in big pleather recliners.

By this point I had seen Paxton deliver his stump speech, a 15-minute case for his Senate candidacy, some half a dozen times. At Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille, his delivery was pained. He seemed tired. He stumbled over his jokes, stopping and returning to the top after realizing he forgot the punch line. He struggled through a section meant to serve as a blistering indictment of his opponent, and he eventually spent several minutes looking down at the podium and listing Talarico’s crimes against Texas off a piece of paper as the crowd sat in silence.

At one point an elderly man with a walker had had enough.

“More enthusiasm!” he shouted from the audience.

Paxton looked up from his papers and out into the crowd. “What?”

“More enthusiasm!” the man shouted again.

“Yes,” Paxton said meekly. “We all need a little more enthusiasm to go to the polls.”

Trump never hesitates to remind voters at his rallies that Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” The candidate has a lazy eye, a casualty of a childhood accident in which a berry was thrown at his face, requiring multiple surgeries, and a subsequent college basketball injury. He presents as meek, almost sheepish, and speaks in a monotone that belies his reputation as a bare-knuckle radical. He slurs his words and stumbles over his lines.

Trump rallied the faithful for Paxton in Corpus Christi.

“Darrell,” he said at one stop, addressing Issa, “California arreddy has tt—you already have two senators, you d—we don’t need a third.” He’s less the guy you want to get a beer with, per the old campaign cliché, and more the guy you feel a bit sorry for when it’s his turn to address the room at a regional sales conference. At a Trump rally for Paxton in Lubbock, the president told the crowd that his praise of Jon Husted’s “very powerful ass” boosted the senator’s election campaign in Ohio. “Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton,” he mused, “but I’m not sure your body is going to qualify.”

For Talarico and the Texas Democrats, who haven’t won a seat in the United States Senate since 1988, the Paxton campaign presents an extraordinary opportunity. “Billy Begala says: For the last 30 years, all you had to do to win in Texas is win the Republican primary and then go on vacation,” said veteran Democratic strategist Paul Begala, whose son Billy works in Texas politics. Paxton may have taken that truism a little too far. After announcing his candidacy for the Republican nomination in an appearance on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show, he “cleared his calendar and booked a hotel in Augusta, Georgia, during the storied Masters golf tournament,” according to the Associated Press, “a trip that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000.” Over July Fourth weekend, while Talarico hit the trail, Paxton was in Europe, sightseeing in London and Iceland with his rumored mistress. As Talarico raised tens of millions of dollars from small-dollar donations throughout the summer, Paxton struggled to keep up. A week before the general election, Talarico had raised $158 million to Paxton’s $39 million.

“Ken is a different type of candidate in modern times,” Bannon said. “He has a hardcore grassroots base, but he’s not a good fundraiser.” In the primary against Cornyn, Paxton “didn’t raise any serious money. This was primarily a grassroots-driven thing.”

Paxton, Bannon added, is “a populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic.”

The last-ditch operation to save the populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic came this week in the form of two Trump rallies. They may end up as the last major events of the campaign. On Thursday, the Paxton campaign announced it was canceling a rally in El Paso scheduled for Sunday, just two days before the election.

At the first of Trump’s appearances, in Corpus Christi, I watched from the press pen as Border Patrol union chief Paul Perez revved up the crowd with a question. “Is Texas Trump country?” he bellowed. A sea of bright red hats, bobbing in chaotic unison in a portside hangar, went ballistic. They had braved the rain and the dour mood spreading across the country to see a president in whom they very much still believed. But across Texas, the cracks in Trump’s support are deepening. Just two years after he beat Kamala Harris in the state by more than 1.5 million votes, The Economist’s poll tracker finds Trump’s approval in Texas is underwater by 18 points. This has fueled fears among the state’s Republicans that many of those who broke for Trump in 2024 could stay home this year or, God forbid, vote for the Democrat who thinks God is nonbinary.

Many rallygoers were decked out in full American flag regalia.

Another’s shirt echoed the Paxton campaign bus.

“Clearly, it has been a challenge for Ken to run during difficult personal times, but one of the reasons we admire him is that he is resilient,” said Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the Conservative Political Action Conference, who held a fundraiser for Paxton at his Virginia home last month. “He will win this race, but, like last time, there will be some fear and trembling along the way.”

Others in the coalition aren’t so sure. “Paxton is in deep shit,” Rich Baris, a pro-Trump pollster, said in a podcast appearance this week.

Trump may rally the base, but it’s hard to see how a historically unpopular president making the race about him helps with the broader electorate. After the president commanded Republicans to host a “Trumpapalooza” midterm convention that served more as a celebration of his presidency than as a typical party congress, Paxton privately told donors the event hurt his campaign. “When we did that convention—it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said, according to audio of his comments obtained by The New York Times. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

At the rally in Corpus Christi, Trump spoke for more than an hour. He extolled the glories of his presidency and made little mention of Paxton. After airing a supercut video of Talarico’s cringiest comments, Trump turned to the crowd. “The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump, thank you!” he said. As the crowd went wild, Trump added: “And I need the help of Paxton.”

On the Come and Take It bus tour, Paxton was less a glimpse of Trumpism’s future than a showcase of what might be left behind when Trump is gone. The familiar accommodations were still required: overlook the scandals, forgive the personal failings, keep faith with the fighter standing between you and the forces of darkness. But there was none of the showmanship that made those demands easier to accept in Trump. The Paxton cocktail is the controversy without the charisma—and a test of whether a record of pure allegiance to Trump is enough for a Republican to win Texas. Defeat may well announce the bitter end of pure Trumpism, or at least prove that Trump alone is the movement. When he leaves the White House in 2029, what will remain of it?

Paxton is not known for his oratory—or his skills as a fundraiser.

One of Natalie Portman’s most iconic roles, even twenty years later, is V For Vendetta. How can one forget how great she looked with a shaved head? She just shared her personal takes on what it was like to be without hair for awhile, I didn’t see this recommendation coming from her.

Portman first rocked a buzzcut in 2005 at the premiere of Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith at Cannes Film Festival. It had been freshly shaven on set when she hopped on a plane to go to the glitzy event in between filming. As she recalled about attending the event with the fresh cut in her words:

Everyone was like, ‘Oh wow, she has no hair.’ And then I went back, got on a plane and went back to Berlin and started shooting again on Monday. It was pretty wild to be out in public exposed like a baby bird. I feel like it's something every woman should do at least once in her life. It feels so amazing to have rain on your head for the first time.

Wow, what a glowing review from Natalie Portman about shaving one’s head! While speaking to Harper’s Bazaar, the actress suggested that “every woman” give it a try at some point in their life. She loved it because it felt amazing to feel the rain on her head – which funny enough is the same thing Millie Bobby Brown pointed out about going bald for Stranger Things. Portman had a really positive review for shaving her head, but there is something she didn’t like so much:

I did not love growing it back. I have curly hair, and so when it grows back you just look like a little boy for a very long time.

Another solid point. I guess there’s always a baseball cap for those awkward growing pains? In V for Vendetta, Portman’s character of Evey has her head shaved against her will when she’s captured, imprisoned and tortured in the dystopian thriller. The moment when her head was shaved off had to be captured in one take with three cameras at once. During rehearsals for the scene, Portman said a bunch of men on the crew offered to have their heads shaved in order for it to be tested and ready for Portman.

Portman is one of quite a few actors who’ve left their hair behind for a while for a role. Emma Stone is the most recent example for her film Bugonia, but in her case, she made her director Yorgos Lanthimos do so too “in solidarity”. Though, the pact wasn’t as satisfying as Stone thought it would be. Florence Pugh also shaved her head for We Live In Time, and has talked about how she was worried she might look like “an egg” before officially committing to it, and embracing the haircut wholeheartedly.

You can check out Natalie Portman in V For Vendetta with a Paramount+ subscription. It’s still arguably one of her best movies, so her bold haircut was absolutely worth it.

#3614. GOG Wants To Bring Back Physical PC Games, But There’s A Catch

While PlayStation 5 console owners are preparing for a discless future, PC gamers have been living in all-digital world for decades now. The advent of Steam and cheaper broadband internet helped end physical PC game sales in the early 2000s, but GOG is dreaming up a future where these games can thrive once again--if it can get past a few obstacles that stand in its way.

Speaking to GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, GOG's senior business development and partnerships manager, laid out a dream scenario in which a consumer can browse GOG, select a game, and have a physical copy delivered to their home. "Ideally, my dream would be to be able to buy physical versions of those games on GOG," Paczynski said. "You go to your shelf on GOG, you click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario."

While that sounds ideal, it's easier said than done, as Paczynski noted that selling physical goods is a logistical challenge when compared to running a digital storefront. Physical media requires organizing storage, delivery, and additional publisher approvals, but Paczynski hopes to see it realized one day.

It's worth noting that the GOG Preservation Program did recently create high-resolution scans for five classic games--Myst, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Star Trek: 25th Anniversary, and Armikrog--and turned them into 3D models that you can view on your PC--as well as printable files for anyone looking for a papercraft project. It's similar to the work done by another site, Big Box Collection, which offers a far larger library of classic PC boxes to admire in 3D.

GOG isn't the only company nostalgic for the big boxes of a bygone era; several sites have popped up in recent years to offer curated collections of physical PC and console games. From Limited Run Games to Special Reserve Games, there's still an appetite for owning something with a tangible quality.

#3613. Everything Eric Dane's Book Reveals About Rebecca Gayheart Relationship

Eric Dane opened up about his history with Rebecca Gayheart — from beginning to end — in his new memoir, My Book of Days.

“We were married for 14 years, grew apart, filed for divorce, but never got around to signing the papers,” Dane wrote in his book, posthumously published Tuesday, November 3. “We’ve since stayed close, coparenting, going on vacations as a family, spending time together, and now we talk every day.”

The pair tied the knot in 2004, later welcoming daughters Billie and Georgia before Gayheart filed for divorce in 2018. They went on to live “separate lives,” according to Dane, but their divorce was never made final.

When Dane was diagnosed with ALS in 2024, Gayheart was one of the first people he called. She supported him and their daughters throughout his health battle until his death earlier this year at age 53.

In the book’s acknowledgements, Dane gave Gayheart a final shout-out, writing, “I can’t thank you enough.”

Scroll down for the biggest revelations about Dane and Gayheart’s relationship from his memoir:

Dane remembered calling Gayheart after finding out his official diagnosis. “I say to Rebecca on the phone, ‘It’s what we feared,'” he wrote. “I don’t remember a single word I said after that. I remember only feeling a violent impact, like getting the wind knocked out of me, and Rebecca wailing on the other end of the phone, and then I really lose it … I hear her words pouring out amid her tears, ‘I’m here, we’ll fight this together, I’m not going anywhere.'”

The actor added, “She will go beyond keeping her word. Rebecca will remain by my side, unwavering, my rock, my champion.”

Dane recalled when he first crossed paths with Gayheart at a party in 1999, noting he was “laser focused” and “gawking” at her while she danced.

“I keep looking at her and, my eyes still on her, I lean down to the woman next to me, a friend, and I say, ‘I’m gonna marry that girl,'” he wrote.

Unfortunately, the friend informed Dane that they were at a party for Gayheart’s then-fiancé. Dane and Gayheart were eventually introduced at the bar and parted ways.

Nearly four years later, the duo happened to bump into each other at a coffee shop. “I glance at her finger. No ring,” Dane recalled.

The pair sparked a “whirlwind romance” over their shared love for sweets and were “pretty much inseparable.”

One day in October 2004, less than a year after their courtship began, Dane mentioned he wanted to get married but wasn’t interested in a wedding. Gayheart agreed, and Dane suggested they go to Las Vegas.

The pair immediately caught a flight and headed to the nearest chapel, asking their cab driver to serve as their witness.

“Rebecca and I look into each other’s eyes and promise that we will love each other until death do us part,” Dane wrote. “OK. A little on the nose. Who knew?”

By 2009, Gayheart “desperately” wanted to have a family, but Dane admitted he was “on the fence” amid his Grey’s Anatomy success.

“We get busy and we get pregnant. But we have a miscarriage,” Dane wrote. “Then we get pregnant again, and we have a second miscarriage. Rebecca starts getting really nervous about time passing, getting older, so we start IVF and we get pregnant a third time — and we have a third miscarriage.”

Though Gayheart thought the losses were “her fault,” Dane got tested and realized he was “the problem.” The pair continued trying to conceive but were unsuccessful — until Dane recommended “a change of scenery.”

“It works,” he wrote, noting that the couple went on a beach getaway. “Rebecca gets pregnant the night we check in.”

Daughters Billie and Georgia were born in 2010 and 2011, respectively.

“Rebecca is the model mom. I thank her every day for the time she puts in, the love and attention she showers on our kids,” Dane wrote later in the book. “I miss out on so much, and that tugs at my heart.”

According to Dane, the pair’s “marriage collapses” around 2018, with Gayheart feeling the weight of his long work hours and “complications” from his addiction battle.

Dane recalled telling a mediator to give Gayheart “whatever she needs” so that there were “no changes” to her life. The duo “move into separate homes” and “live separate lives,” but Dane admitted that their dynamic wasn’t conventional.

“We leave our marriage, but we don’t leave our family,” he wrote. “Rebecca and I are not a couple anymore. Well, except sometimes, when we can’t help ourselves. Usually, almost always, we’re not a couple. But we are, always, a family.”

For Dane, it seemed “pretty straightforward” to get along for their children. Gayheart had full custody, with their daughters living with her to eliminate “schlepping back and forth from house to house.” They continued to spend holidays as a family and travel together, which Dane thought their kids found “confusing.”

Dane and Gayheart carried on with their lives, but divorce papers were never filed. “I contend that we simply forget,” he wrote.

Dane commended Gayheart for staying by his side as his health declined, calling her his “best friend.”

“She drops by every day, early in the morning, late at night, sometimes in the middle of the night when she knows I won’t be sleeping,” he wrote. “She’s the person I call, the one I go to when I need to talk, when I need to scream, when I need to cry.”

#3612. Borderlands Franchise Hits 100 Million Sales As Gearbox Hints At What’s Next

The Borderlands franchise has reached a new sales milestone, as developer Gearbox Software announced that Borderlands 4 had pushed the series over the 100 million units sold mark. Celebrating the achievement, the studio also took time to reveal what's next for Borderlands 4 as it enters its second year, as well as plans it's busy cooking up for the IP.

"We just wrapped our Year 1 roadmap, and the team is cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year," Gearbox wrote in a blog post, adding that weekly activity refreshes and Community Challenges will continue in the game. So what's next for Borderlands? Gearbox says that it's "a bigger look at the franchise as a whole," and it's also listening to fans to gauge which characters they want to spend more time with.

Don't expect Gearbox to drop a Borderlands 5 announcement anytime soon, as the developer said it needs time and space to work on future projects. "Big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we’ll talk more when the time is right," Gearbox added. Thirteen months ago, Gearbox Software boss Randy Pitchford had predicted that Borderlands 4 would continue to sell millions of copies and would help the franchise cross the 100 million units sold line eventually. "We will break 100 million units with this launch, easily, all in, with the franchise," Pitchford said at the time.

To put that in perspective, the Borderlands franchise had sold 94 million units through August 2025, meaning Borderlands 4 would move at least 6 million copies. Historically, Borderlands 2 is the franchise's top seller, with 31 million units sold, while Borderlands 3 is second with 23 million sales to date. It's worth noting that these games have also gone on sale regularly--with Borderlands 3 once being sold for just $3 on PC via Steam--and Borderlands 4 has also received a few discounts since launch. Gearbox and publisher Take-Two Interactive haven't revealed sales figures for Borderlands 4 yet, so it's hard to know where it currently fits on the Borderlands sales chart.

The game didn't have a smooth launch either, as various technical hurdles required multiple rounds of patching, and the oft-delayed Switch 2 edition was eventually paused so that Gearbox could focus on the PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S editions of the game.

#3611. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.
