Mckenna Grace has been working since she was a little kid, and at 20 years old, it feels like she’s done a bit of everything. She’s done drama, action, horror, romance and more, and in her next project, the book-to-screen adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping, she’ll play out a deeply intense tragedy that also features massive action. However, while it’s clear she’s open to many kinds of projects and work, there is one thing she says no to: nudity. Surprisingly, her reasoning has to do with Disney.

As I said, when it comes to Grace's career, she's explored lots of different genres, which have put her in many different situations. I mean, in the last year alone, she’s worked on Regretting You, Five Nights at Freddy’s 2, Scream 7, PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie, The Last Kiss, Nimrods and Sunrise on the Reaping. Those are all very different movies, and during an interview with Cosmopolitan, she was asked if there are any kinds of roles she’d say no to. Here’s how she responded, and how nudity and Disney came into the conversation:

At this point, I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things. I respect anybody who can, but it’s terrifying to me. I don’t know if that’ll ever change. It’s not like I only do wholesome things—my character literally gets gutted by Ghostface in Scream—but my dream is to try and be a Disney princess someday.

See, it’s obvious from her explanation that she has nothing against intimacy or nudity. And it seems like she has a lot of respect for actors who do work on projects that require it or very sexual sequences, like Off Campus, for example. However, it’s not her cup of tea, and I do see why.

As she said, she wants to be a Disney princess someday. If you’ve seen the best Disney movies, you know there’s a certain level of wholesomeness involved. That’s not to say an actor who participates in a project that involves sex scenes or nudity wouldn’t get a role as a Disney princess or prince. However, it’s clear Grace is trying to create an image for herself that makes her an unquestionable fit for one of these very wholesome roles.

I think she’s doing a good job at that too. I mean, before Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim were cast as Rapunzel and Flynn Rider for the live-action Tangled, Mckenna Grace and Mason Thames were popular fan casts for the parts. She legitimately looks like a princess, and her bubbly and bright personality fits right in with that kind of character too.

Now, getting back to what she said, she made it clear she’s not only going to do wholesome roles, and her work on the 2026 movie schedule clearly showcases that. I mean, Scream 7 is a horror movie, and as she said, she gets brutally murdered in it. Also, Sunrise on the Reaping is not for the faint of heart. As a fan of the book, I know how brutal the story is, and I know we’ll see Grace acting out some truly violent and intense moments.

However, while she’s willing to do work like that, she does have boundaries she does not want to cross. That means she’ll say no to projects that are hypersexual or involve nudity, which is totally respectable.

With that said, hopefully someday she’ll get her wish of being a Disney princess. While we wait for that to happen (because I do feel like it’s inevitable), you can catch Mckenna Grace in Sunrise on the Reaping on November 20.

#3547. Parties That Changed the World: Barbie’s Premiere and Gone With the Wind’s Debut

The world’s most famous doll was inspired by a spunky, high-end call girl named Lilli. Described as a “gold digger, exhibitionist, and floozy,” the character of Bild Lilli was created in 1952 by German cartoonist Reinhard Beuthien after he was asked to draw a filler cartoon for the inaugural issue of the tabloid Bild-Zeitung. Lilli, a buxom blonde with a perky ponytail and sky-high stilettos, sat beside a fortune teller. “Can’t you give me the name and address of this tall, handsome, rich man?” she cooed. The cartoon was an instant hit, and in 1955, Lilli was immortalized in plastic.

A year later, Ruth Handler discovered the Lilli doll while on a vacation in Europe. She bought several. One was for her teenage daughter, Barbara, to keep; the rest were brought back to Mattel, the toy company she had cofounded with her husband, Elliot, and businessman Harold Matson. (Mattel is a portmanteau of both men’s names.) Lilli—with comically large breasts, chic outfits, and heavy makeup—was precisely what Handler had been looking for.

Robin Gerber, author of Barbie and Ruth, wrote: “The doll looked too much like a prostitute for the company’s taste,” so Mattel’s design team (slightly) softened Lilli’s exaggerated proportions, renamed her Barbie, after Barbara, and before long, she would become the physical ideal for generations of young girls and women everywhere.

Sixty-four years after Barbie hit shelves, she finally got her close-up in Barbie, a feminist manifesto in a pair of pink stilettos. The film’s premiere and after-party at the Shrine Auditorium marked Warner Bros.’ largest premiere to date—and the cherry on top of a bubble-gum-flavored, years-long marketing blitz. According to Event Marketer, “the affair was like Barbie herself: high-energy, glamorous and very, very, colorful.”

It was a beautiful day in Hollywood. Even by Los Angeles standards, the weather on Sunday, July 9, 2023, was almost impossibly perfect—sunshine, low 70s, and a cool breeze—as if Hollywood itself has been dropped into the fantasy world of Barbie Land.

The event kicked off with a splash. The pink carpet was tricked out with replicas of pieces from the film’s beach scenes: a lifeguard station, a towering lighthouse, faux palm trees, and a 3D ocean wave, with carpeting that shifted colors to mimic sand. A wide range of influencers were invited to get first dibs on photo ops before the stars arrived. But the real showstopper was the two-story replica of Barbie’s Dreamhouse, complete with a 2D faux pool, a DJ spinning tracks, and the trademark spiral slide. “We had to have that slide,” Wendy Robino, SVP of Warner Bros. marketing events, said at the time.

On Sunday, they wore pink: Writer and director Greta Gerwig, along with cast members Issa Rae, America Ferrera, Kate McKinnon, Ryan Gosling, and Michael Cera, turned out for the premiere in every shade of Barbie’s signature color, turning something long dismissed as girly into a celebration of individuality, joy, and girl power.

But the belle of the ball wasn’t one to blend in. After weeks of thinking pink, Margot Robbie—the film’s star and producer—arrived in black. Her custom Schiaparelli look re-created 1960s’ Solo in the Spotlight Barbie: a black sequined dress with a single red rose stitched onto her tulle skirt, matching opera gloves, Manolo Blahnik mules, and a diamond necklace. Movie Star Barbie fully committed to the bit, even clutching a pink handkerchief as she posed in front of a pink Corvette. Robbie’s blond hair was swept into a high ponytail—reminiscent of the one first worn by Lilli.

Following the official screening—marking the first time Barbie was revealed to the public—it was time to party.

The theme was “Barbie’s Blowout Disco Party.” Fittingly, one attraction invited guests inside a glittering, 12-foot pink disco ball. Justin Lefkovitch, whose company Mirrored Media, partnered with Mattel to create it, tells VF the entrance created “a shroud of mystery” for partygoers. Inside, a six-foot 1:1 Dreamhouse showcasing the new Barbie the Movie doll collection was surrounded by gold and silver streamers and over a dozen custom pink disco balls. The goal, Lefkovitch recalls, was to “transport guests into the world of Barbie.”

Nicki Minaj was the first guest to arrive at the party, event producer Austin Johnston tells VF—“five-foot-long hair all the way down to the floor.” A theme park designer by trade, Johnston and his company, AKJohnston, transformed the after-party into what he calls a “pop-up museum.” Barbie Land’s pastel-colored cul-de-sac was re-created as “a 65-foot-tall, 70-foot-wide” inflatable, its landmarks crammed together like a kitschy postcard. At the end of Barbie’s driveway, Mark Ronson presided over a hot pink DJ booth, playing hits from the soundtrack by Ice Spice, Dua Lipa (a.k.a. Mermaid Barbie), and Nicki Minaj—whom Johnston had to “very kindly” ask to get off Barbie’s Corvette.

Tucked beneath the second-floor mezzanine, a series of alcoves became larger-than-life photo sets, with photographers on hand to capture guests in action. Partygoers could retrace Barbie’s journey to the Real World—by bike, boat, and rocket ship—or step inside the Kendom man cave, Weird Barbie’s house, and life-size Barbie and Ken toy boxes. Not everyone hired to re-create Barbie Land had actually seen the movie by then; only a handful were invited to be part of that “really restricted small group,” Johnston says.

At the center of the room, guests sipped pink cocktails under a giant disco ball while an 11-foot, glitter-coated pink B twirled above. Another bar doubled as a fashion show, with four life-size mannequins dolled up for disco in original costumes from the film’s dance number, including Barbie’s gold sequined jumpsuit and the Kens’ matching white-and-gold tracksuits.

Obviously, the food was on theme too. Wolfgang Puck catered the evening’s Barbie-Q, serving grilled salmon, summer melon salad, roasted Pink Fir apple potatoes, char siu glazed grilled chicken, and charred tricolor cauliflower.

Even the night’s corporate sponsors knew better than to steal Barbie’s spotlight. OPI set up a nail salon, and Xbox provided a gaming station where players had their pick of two General Motors rides: Barbie’s Corvette or Ken’s Hummer. A highlight for Johnston was spotting Robbie racing a virtual Hummer while her Australian parents cheered her on. “No one paid her to do that,” he says. “She’s just like, I want to have a drink and play a video game at my premiere.”

For one night in Hollywood, women could be anything. And 84 years earlier, another city had hosted another rager in honor of another larger-than-life heroine. While Los Angeles turned pink for Barbie, Atlanta resurrected the Old South for Scarlett O’Hara.

All hell broke loose when British actor Vivien Leigh was cast as beloved heroine Scarlett O’Hara in the big-screen adaptation of Margaret Mitchell’s epic, Gone With the Wind. Fans and journalists were outraged that such an iconic Southern Belle would be played by a foreigner. At the time, Leigh was yet to star in a Hollywood film and was best known stateside for her affair with Laurence Olivier. Gossip columnist Hedda Hopper sniped: “Out of millions of American women, [producer David O. Selznick] couldn’t find one to suit him.”

Hopper was exaggerating, but not by a lot: During a grueling two-year nationwide search for his leading lady, Selznick reportedly met with over 1,400 actresses. After angry fan letters poured in, Selznick’s publicity machine kicked into overdrive—and eventually, the public came around to the idea that a refined Brit was somehow easier to swallow than a Yankee.

But perhaps the most convincing endorsement came from Leigh’s own leading man. Even Clark Gable, who initially considered Leigh “too demure” for the Southern firecracker, was won over by her dedication and declared she “was Scarlett every minute.” His own casting, meanwhile, had been a dream come true from the thousands who flooded MGM and Selznick’s offices with letters demanding he play Rhett Butler

The shoot was famously plagued by drama, and by the time filming wrapped, the cast and crew had earned themselves a party.

But Selznick had bigger fish to fry—namely, finishing the movie in time for its premiere. He left the party planning to local organizers and his trusted story editor Kay Brown, who had convinced her boss to buy the film rights in the first place. But since Atlanta was still tightly in the grip of Jim Crow, not everyone could join in. Leigh’s costars Hattie McDaniel and Butterfly McQueen were excluded from the festivities.

Selznick argued, unsuccessfully, with local organizers to get McDaniel on the guest list. Gable threatened to not attend the premiere in solidarity with his friend, The Hollywood Reporter stated, but McDaniel ultimately talked him out of it. “While it was unfortunate to exclude Mammy, it was the wisest policy,” Brown wrote, per Matthew Bernstein, former professor of film and media studies at Emory University.

Meanwhile, white Atlanta was gearing up for the party of the century. Former president Jimmy Carter later called it the South’s “biggest event” in his lifetime. According to Time, then governor Eurith D. Rivers was prepared to call in the National Guard, while Mayor Hartsfield urged every woman of Atlanta to dust off her hoop skirts and each man to “sprout a goatee, sideburns, and Kentucky colonel whiskers.”

Hollywood came in hot. Leigh and Gable made their grand entrance by limousine, waving to the 300,000 spectators who lined seven miles of streets in downtown Atlanta—including a number of nonagenarian Confederate veterans who were invited as special guests. Leigh arrived with Olivier while Gable brought his new wife, Carole Lombard. Fun fact: Gable reportedly hadn’t even wanted to play Rhett Butler until Louis B. Mayer offered to help bankroll his divorce so he could marry Lombard.

Of the motorcade, Time wrote: “Crowds larger than the combined armies that fought at Atlanta in July 1864 waved Confederate flags, tossed confetti till it seemed to be snowing, gave three different versions of the Rebel yell, whistled, cheered, goggled.” Leigh wept as the crowd welcomed the British actress “back home,” as if she’d just returned from battle.

The multiday event included a costume ball thrown by the Junior League that would have Abraham Lincoln rolling over in his grave. Decked out in hoop skirts, bustles, and Confederate-era uniforms, 6,000 guests descended on the Municipal Auditorium, which had been transformed into a recreation of the film’s Monster Bazaar. Black participants were relegated to serving or entertaining. Among them was the Ebenezer Baptist Church choir, whose singers reportedly performed dressed as enslaved people in front of a façade of Tara, a fictional plantation from the film. One of the singers was 10-year-old future civil rights hero Martin Luther King Jr.

Vivien Leigh arrived in a velvet gown designed by Walter Plunkett. Though Olivier escorted her costar Olivia de Havilland instead—to keep up appearances—Leigh was the belle of the ball, especially in hometown hero Margaret Mitchell’s absence. Eighteen years earlier, the young novelist had performed a risqué “apache dance” at a charity gala, which cost her her Junior League membership. Now, with Hollywood celebrating her masterpiece, some suspected Mitchell was getting the last laugh by snubbing the biggest party in town.

Young women fangirled all over Gable. According to Time, one woman fainted at the sight of him. Another was given a choice: a Christmas gift or a chance to meet the heartthrob. She chose Gable. After he kissed the 11-year-old, she gasped, “Now am I a woman?”

Governor Rivers declared December 15, 1939, a statewide holiday in honor of Gone With the Wind’s world premiere, the grand finale of the three-day extravaganza. Searchlights swept the Southern sky, and flashbulbs popped as 18,000 spectators crowded Peachtree Street. Even Loew’s Grand Theater got a glow-up. Its Romanesque façade was disguised as a grand Southern plantation—four towering white columns were erected to support a temporary façade with floral garlands, potted trees, and an enormous portrait of Leigh and Gable hung above the entrance.

Inside, all 2,000-plus seats sold out at $10 a pop—the equivalent of about $240 today. That’s not exactly chump change, considering Atlanta was still licking its wounds after the Great Depression. Young women in antebellum costumes greeted guests before Mayor Hartsfield took the stage to kick things off. Selznick and the film’s stars received standing ovations that lasted a full minute. But the loudest cheers were for Mitchell, now in attendance, who joined Leigh and Gable onstage.

The lights dimmed for nearly four hours of melodrama. When Rhett Butler delivered his immortal parting shot—“Frankly, my dear, I don’t give a damn”—the audience reportedly gasped, then erupted in applause as he left Scarlett in his dust.

Before Gone With the Wind—still the highest-grossing film of all time when adjusted for inflation—premieres were usually exclusive screenings in Hollywood or New York. 1939’s antebellum extravaganza turned an entire city into a movie set, setting the stage for modern spectacles like Barbie.

Both parties also offer a revealing snapshot of the societies that threw them. For Gone With the Wind, the industry glorified an imagined past; for Barbie, Hollywood toasted an imagined future. The Barbie premiere wasn’t just a love letter to a feminist film: It was also a giant corporate juggernaut designed to sell a product whose history was tangled up with the very stereotypes the film was questioning. It paid off: Following the film’s theatrical release, Mattel reported a third-quarter increase in worldwide gross billings of 27%, and Barbie toy sales in the United States increased 25% for the July-August combined months compared to the same two-month period a year prior. The immersive premiere, brand collaborations, worldwide activations, and fan participation blurred the line between marketing a movie and creating a cultural event.

The film also became Warner Bros.’ most successful release of all time, grossing $1.4 billion worldwide and making Greta Gerwig the first solo female director admitted into the hallowed halls of the billion-dollar boys club. The premiere celebrated a movie that changed the cultural conversation while handily outgrossing the testosterone-fueled Oppenheimer—a spectacular rebuke to the assumption that chick flicks have a glass ceiling.

Its timing made the celebration particularly potent. In that moment, Hollywood was still finding its footing after the pandemic; the premiere offered something audiences were missing. “It eventized going back to the movies. It eventized the premiere,” says Lefkovitch.

For one night, partygoers got to revel in a fairy tale where women ruled the world. But outside Barbie Land, the irony had all the subtlety of Ken’s Mojo Dojo Casa House. Hollywood was throwing an enormous party celebrating a fantasy of female empowerment while women were still fighting for equality in the real world. There is “definitely some hypocrisy,” agrees Lefkovitch, who made a point of thanking his all-female team.

Decades earlier, Atlanta had thrown its own enormous party, celebrating a fantasy of Southern womanhood while reinforcing the racial and social hierarchies of the real South—and conveniently leaving the horrors of slavery out of the picture. (The film itself did just that, presenting a fictional plantation where the most loyal individuals enjoyed being enslaved.) Black performers were welcome to entertain white audiences, but not to celebrate alongside them; not a single seat inside Loew’s Grand Theater was available to Black moviegoers.

Together, these indignities galvanized the local Black press. In a column for Atlanta Daily World, Reverend John Clarence Wright wrote, “As Atlanta goes mad with the Wind one hundred thousand of her citizens should become more thoughtful than ever of the course that must be pursued to gain their rights as free men and citizens in a land where the spirit of secession and slavery still lives.” With Black moviegoers barred from Southern theaters, the Pittsburgh Courier dryly observed, “Negro reaction… will have to wait until the film comes North.”

The premiere and the film’s success helped propel the NAACP to fight not just individual films, but toward a broader campaign to change Hollywood itself. In 1942, NAACP leader Walter White spoke directly to studio heads in an attempt to persuade them to steer away from demeaning Black stereotypes—like the ones onscreen in Gone With the Wind—and to increase the roles available to Black actors in Hollywood.

White’s approach infuriated the very woman whose absence from the Atlanta premiere had helped expose Hollywood’s hypocrisy: Hattie McDaniel. As a Black woman, McDaniel’s choices were limited—“I’d rather play a maid than be one,” she once said. Writing for Vanity Fair, Hadley Hall Meares noted that McDaniel was “incensed” that White had negotiated with the studios on her behalf, and believed she and her fellow Black actors deserved their own seat at the negotiating table.

McDaniel did get a seat at the 1940 Oscars—but it was at a small table at the edge of the room, separated from her Gone With the Wind costars. The ceremony, after all, was held at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub, which had a strict color line. When her name was called, McDaniel gushed: “I sincerely hope I shall always be a credit to my race and to the motion picture industry.”

Meares described McDaniel’s life as “a tightrope walk.” She was expected to satisfy the white executives who controlled her career, the Black audiences who wanted better representation, and her own ambitions as an actress.

Vivien Leigh also made history that night, becoming the first Brit to win the Oscar for best actress. She dedicated her award to Selznick for his “energy, courage, and very great kindness.” After all, he had been partly responsible for convincing an initially outraged public that Leigh was worthy to play their beloved Scarlett O’Hara. Years later, the Academy lavished Barbie with eight nominations, though it snubbed Gerwig for best director and Robbie for best actress. (Frankly, my dear, they didn’t give a damn about the two women who created Barbie Land.) If Hollywood could build an entire universe in which women ruled the world, why was it still so difficult to imagine one outside the movie theater?

Billie Eilish and Finneas O’Connell took home Barbie’s only Oscar, for best original song. Their winning composition poses Barbie’s existential question while echoing the expectations heaped upon Scarlett, Leigh, McDaniel, Robbie, and Gerwig: “What Was I Made For?”

It turns out the inspiration for Barbie—the quintessential American toy—wasn’t even made for little girls. Lilli dolls were sold to grown men in European tobacco shops and adult toy stores, becoming popular gag gifts. “Men… put them on their car dashboard, dangled them from the rearview mirror, or gave them to girlfriends as a suggestive keepsake,” Gerber wrote. Long before Barbie could be anything, she was something for men.

Eighty-four years apart, Hollywood threw two spectacular parties for women who refused to play by the rules. But the rules were still very much in place when the lights came back up.

The long wait for All’s Fair’s second season is finally almost over. The Ryan Murphy legal drama is set to return on Wednesday on the 2026 TV schedule, nearly a year after Season 1 ended. Not surprisingly, the cast is making headlines ahead of the new season, and also not surprisingly, everyone is talking about the corset dress Kim Kardashian wore to the premiere. However, can we please talk about Teyana Taylor’s fit, too?

On Monday, Hulu hosted a premiere for All’s Fair Season 2, and the fashion was absolutely on point. Kardashian, as usual, turned heads as she wore a custom Ashi Studio silver strapless corset dress with a matching silver collar, per Law Roach's Instagram. She posted the look on her Instagram Story, and I am positively obsessed:

That being said, her co-star Teyana Taylor might be giving her a run for her money. The Oscar-nominated actress has also been making waves in the world of celebrity fashion, leaving no crumbs at the BET Awards over the summer by rocking a stunning burgundy Stephanie Rolland gown. Now, once again, she proved that she’s a fashion icon at the All’s Fair premiere with a daring low-rise ensemble:

The look is from Nicholas Oakwell Couture, per Women’s Wear Daily. Between the corset sheer top, the large bow over the black pants, and the bolero jacket, the entire ensemble is incredible. You never know what you’re going to get when it comes to Taylor, and she definitely made that point clear with this look. Of course, Kardashian looked great as well; however, the One Battle After Another actress definitely has my vote for best dressed.

However, I have to say that Kardashian and Taylor’s friendship makes this pair of outfits even better. The Rip actress previously opened up about her friendship with the reality star, pointing out that they were already friends before All's Fair. However, she said that doing this series together “really brought [them] closer.” She continued, “We really went into the show friends and finished out the show as sisters.”

Now, fans will be seeing more of that friendship in the upcoming second season of All’s Fair. Kardashian will return as Allura Grant, while Taylor will once again be playing Milan in the Hulu hit. In the new season, there will be plenty more scandals, secrets, and stilettos, as new allegiances are formed, friendships are tested, and a “shocking revelation threatens the very existence” of Grant, Ronson & Greene.

Meanwhile, since All’s Fair has pulled off some incredible fashion in the show, it’s understandable that the cast would want to do the same IRL. Now, I need Teyana Taylor to do another red carpet, because I can only imagine what she and her stylists have planned next. And the same goes for Kim K.

Now, to see the two women in All's Fair, you can stream Season 2 this Wednesday, November 4, with a Hulu subscription.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

#3545. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3544. David Baldacci, John Grisham, and Scott Turow Know How a Story Can End. They Say Losing the Rule of Law to Trump Would Be a “Death Sentence for America”

In July, for the first time in seven years, sitting justices of the US Supreme Court testified at the Capitol. Chief Justice John Roberts has been shy about letting members of the Court answer legislators’ questions, viewing it as a violation of the separation of powers. However, in this case, there was apparently no choice, since the Supreme Court requested millions of dollars to enhance its very own security in the face of sharply growing threats to lower court judges—threats that have grown exponentially over the last decade.

We are all lawyers as well as novelists. We have appeared in court on various matters before both judges and juries, and thus believe that respect for the rule of law is absolutely essential to have any hope for a civilized society. Recent events, like the reasons for justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett to testify before Congress, have prompted us to write this, because we want all Americans to understand that we are drawing perilously close to the rule of law becoming optional. For any free and open democracy, not only is that unacceptable, but it is a death sentence for America.

Respect for the rule of law must come from everyone, and it most certainly should come from the highest officeholder in the land. Unfortunately, with the current administration, we have witnessed the exact opposite result.

Donald Trump with Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, and Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett in February 2026.

Consider the fundamental text: The Declaration of Independence, which celebrated its 250th anniversary this year—and established what the framers viewed as the bedrock principles for a just government, starting with the declaration’s most hallowed statement, that all persons are created equal. But the document went on to list many grievances against the tyrannical rule of King George III, including the fact that the king had made “Judges dependent on his Will alone,” because it was solely the king’s grace that decided their continued employment or compensation. In response, our Constitution tried to insulate the federal judiciary from outside influence by providing for lifetime appointments.

But fast-forward to the present day, and President Donald Trump has repeatedly demeaned and insulted judges, variously claiming that a judge’s heritage, religion, or political affiliation can compromise their legal judgement. In February, he flagrantly labeled the members of the Supreme Court who had voted to overrule his tariffs as “fools and lapdogs,” claiming they were “swayed by foreign interests,” and attacking Neil Gorsuch and Coney Barrett, two of the justices he himself had appointed, calling them “an embarrassment to their families.”

Even more egregiously, the Trump administration has gone beyond schoolyard insults to taking actions that actually circumvent the rule of law.

For example, Trump’s use of the Justice Department to bring criminal prosecutions against those he thinks wronged him personally is one of his most brazen acts of defiance of established legal norms. The indictments of former FBI director James Comey, whom Trump fired, and Letitia James, the New York attorney general who brought a successful civil fraud case against Trump, his children, and Trump family businesses, were both thrown out of court because Trump’s selection of one of his former personal lawyers as the prosecutor was found illegal. The newest prosecution of Comey, because of a supposedly threatening arrangement of seashells on a beach, is equally unlikely to stand up under prevailing law.

The Ábrego Garcia matter is another instance of abuse, because it dramatizes the disobedience by the Trump administration with respect to immigration court orders. Kilmar Armando Ábrego Garcia was deported to the Salvadorean mega-prison despite being legally present in the US. The government first refused to return him, claiming, without adequate proof, that he was a member of the criminal organization MS-13. However, once the pressure became too much, he was returned to the US. Only then did the Justice Department charge him with human smuggling, claiming he had transported people within the US who were in the country unlawfully. His case was dismissed by the trial judge on the grounds of vindictive and selective prosecution and remains on appeal.

We are, without a doubt, in the midst of a veritable plague of looming dangers aimed squarely at the judiciary. Not only did an armed man attempt to assassinate Justice Brett Kavanaugh at his home in 2022 following a leak of the Dobbs decision, hostile threats directed at judges have more than tripled over the past decade, according to Chief Justice Roberts’s 2024 year-end report. Citing statistics from the US Marshals Service, the report said that in the past five years alone, more than 1,000 serious threats were investigated, and dozens of people were charged with crimes. In 2020, the US Marshals said it responded to over 4,000 threats or inappropriate communications against federal judges. In that same year, a disgruntled lawyer murdered US District Judge Esther Salas’s son and wounded her husband after gaining access to their home by posing as a delivery person. According to NBC News, in 2025, there were 103 unordered pizza deliveries to judges who had ruled against the Trump administration or spoke out about threats against the judiciary, and 20 were sent in Salas’s name.

As novelists, for decades, we have all explored themes of corruption, influence peddling, and pressure and threats against public servants in our fiction.

In Scott’s latest novel, Presumed Guilty, about a murder trial in a rural area in the upper Midwest, the longtime prosecutor, Hiram Jackdorp, and the trial judge, Wendy Carrington, have a contentious relationship. Jackdorp forced her out of his office when she was a young prosecutor, and later unsuccessfully attempted to prevent her election to the bench. But there is no moment during the trial when the novel’s narrator, the defense lawyer Rusty Sabich, sees Judge Carrington’s rulings as based on anything but a fair application of legal principles. She is a good judge whose fidelity to the rule of law prevents her from using her position for personal revenge.

In John’s 2008 novel The Appeal, an ambitious young attorney is unwittingly recruited by some nefarious special interests to seek election to the state supreme court. Their big money pours in and buys enough votes. He wins, unseats a legendary jurist, and takes office. But when the pay-off comes due, he realizes that his judicial independence is far more important than playing politics.

In David’s 1996 novel Absolute Power, an American president presumes himself to be above the rule of law and seeks to force his underlings to commit criminal acts that will benefit him. However, the institutions created to check and prevent just such abuses hold fast against these brazen king-like attempts to be immune from baldly unlawful actions. At the end of the novel the truth is revealed, and the criminal justice system holds the president appropriately accountable for his misdeeds.

The “rule of law” is not simply a slogan the three of us learned in law school, or a plot device we use in our fiction. It is what keeps our life in society from turning into the war of all against all, where laws that allow for a civilized way of life matter little and violence and chaos reign. It’s also what keeps our economy vibrant and growing.

Without the fair enforcement of the laws being sacrosanct, economic decline inevitably follows as investors decide against investing in American businesses, building plants or factories here, or purchasing American corporate or government bonds and other investment vehicles. If there is no certainty that commercial contracts or international trade agreements will be honored, this will also vastly diminish the potential of any economy. And if the environment is one where an unbiased court is not the final arbiter of legal disputes, our allies may well think twice before committing resources and lasting cooperation since the environment they sought to work and invest within could change without regard to legality. Economic decline invariably leads to widespread job losses, a lessening standard of living, a loss of confidence in institutions by the citizens, our allies stampeding away from us, and a dilution of every individual right outlined in the Constitution.

And it’s not just us who are worried. There are many other lawyers and judges who have expressed concern about the trajectory of this country to ignore court rulings if they collide with political expediency or partisan goals. Nonpartisan organizations like Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition initiative and the Democracy Rising Collaborative have brought together retired judges and advocates to sound the alarm over a country in peril.

What we are all advocating for is that the courts be given the respect they are due under the founding documents of this country. Article I of the United States Constitution established the legislative branch, the United States Congress. Article II established the executive branch, headed up by the presidency. Article III created the US Supreme Court, and granted the power to Congress to establish lower federal courts.

In the 1803 ruling of Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court asserted that the courts had the power of judicial review, and with that power came the ability to declare laws passed by the Congress as being unconstitutional. This one ruling lifted the judicial branch to full equality with the other branches, because their decisions would constitute the final ruling on whether or not something was legal or constitutional and in agreement with our rights protected under the Constitution.

In order to be fair and objective arbiters of the law, federal courts must be free from influence, bias, and manipulation from outside sources. There can be no middle ground here. The courts are either free to do their work or they are not.

Each time a court order is ignored or defied, a sliver of independence is torn from the judicial robe. If the executive branch’s answer to a ruling it does not like is simply to not enforce it, or to encourage disobedience through open disrespect, then the independence of the judiciary evaporates. Not only does the legal system itself suffer from this noncompliance, but every citizen does as well, because if one branch of government can defy and ignore court decisions, that means they can potentially defy and ignore the individual rights of any American citizen.

The rule of law must be respected, and the valid decisions of courts must be upheld by the government, even, and perhaps most importantly, when that ruling goes against the government. Only in that way can a free and independent judiciary continue to deliver the ideals outlined in the founding documents of what is the most durable democracy ever conceived and created. Without that, America can no longer claim to be the shining beacon on the hill, inspiring democracy the world over. We, in fact, will become the opposite of what this country has always stood for. Even with our combined imaginations, we can envision no greater tragedy.

Grey's Anatomy is one of the most legendary medical dramas of all time, and we're currently in its whopping 23rd season on ABC (and streaming with a Hulu subscription). The beloved medical drama is till going strong, but many fans like to look back at its glory days. Late actor Eric Dane famously played Mark Sloane/ McSteamy during that time, and excerpts from his posthumous memoir got honest about his struggles during that time.

McSteamy is one of the most beloved Grey's character of all time, in no small part thanks to the charisma and heart that Dane brought to the role. In his recently released memoir My Book of Days (via EW) he wrote about an injury and reliance on painkillers resulted in him deteriorating during his time at Seattle Grace Hospital. He wrote:

My body goes to shit. I drop to 170, my face caves in, my eyes cloud, I look gaunt; shit, I look like a drug addict. You can tell. I can tell. My attitude on set changes. I’m no longer bubbly, the fun guy, a ringleader in laughs. I don’t act out. I don’t throw tantrums or chairs. I go the other way. I bring everything inside. I dissolve.

What a heartbreaking recollection. While Grey's fans were still head over heels in love with Sloan, Dane was having a private struggle with his health and substances that was making his job difficult. Rather than acting out he felt himself "dissolving", and not letting it impact this coworkers. Indeed, Grey's Anatomy stars wrote tributes to the late actor following his tragic death in February.

Later in his memoir, the Euphoria star does mention that his coworkers noticed the change in him. He wrote about the dynamic he felt at the time, in a section which reads:

I can’t help it. I feel other members of the cast looking at me. They’re my friends. My work family. No. My family. They don’t judge me. They don’t look angry. They look concerned. They look sad.

It's tough to hear how Eric Dane was struggling during this time, and how he was being so private about it while bringing McSteamy to life. He didn't want to bother his co-workers and chosen family, but they noticed that something was going on. That includes the one and only Shonda Rhimes, who did offer to help the Last Ship actor. As he wrote:

I tell her I’m dealing with it. I lie to her. I lie to myself. I suck it up. Fight through it. I don’t want to be Shonda’s burden. I don’t want to be a problem. But I am. I am a problem.

Clearly Eric Dane took the time to reflect on his years on Grey's Anatomy, and the struggles he was dealing with at the time. In his book he was able to speak honestly about his issues, and take responsibility for being a "problem." It's a powerful testament, one that might help inspire readers who are dealing with similar issues.

New episodes of Grey's Anatomy air Thursdays on ABC as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Folks who want to re-watch Dane's iconic tenure as McSteamy can do so on both Hulu and Netflix. Although after hearing about his experience, it might hit differently.

#3542. 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Director’s Next Movie Officially Picked up by Sony

Lionsgate is teaming up with Sony for Destin Daniel Cretton's anime adaptation

The live-action Naruto movie is officially moving forward, thanks to some help from Sony. The anime adaptation from Destin Daniel Cretton (Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Short Term 12) has been in the works at Lionsgate and is now set to begin production next year. This marks yet another collaboration between Cretton and Sony, a partnership that saw massive success this year with the latest Tom Holland Spider-Man movie.

In an official press release, Lionsgate announced that Sony Pictures will co-finance and distribute Naruto internationally following a highly competitive bidding war. With Sony onboard, Lionsgate has now greenlit the project and scheduled production to start in spring 2027. Lionsgate will oversee the movie's development, production, and domestic distribution.

Destin Daniel Cretton will write, direct, and produce. On reuniting with Cretton for Naruto, Sony Pictures CEO Tom Rothman said that "we had a sweet success this summer with Destin and are delighted to be back in his capable hands," also calling Lionsgate's project an A-level adaptation. Following the success of Brand New Day this year, Sony entered a three-year deal in which Cretton will develop and produce films for the company under Hisako, the production company he runs with Jeyun Munford.

The live-action film will be based on the series by Masashi Kishimoto, which has become a global sensation across manga, anime, and video games. Naruto follows the titular character, who starts the story as a young orphan in a fantasy world inspired by Japan's feudal era. Naruto dreams of becoming Hokage, essentially the village leader, and pursues that dream alongside an ever-expanding supporting cast.

This July, Cretton announced that a global casting search for the film had begun to find the series' main trio (called Team 7): Naruto, Sasuke, and Sakura. While Lionsgate and Cretton haven't confirmed any casting yet, it has also been reported that Charles Melton (Beef) is in talks for the role of Kakashi, Team 7's mentor.

#3540. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

Since Patrick Stewart's death became public knowledge nearly a week ago, many across social media have been taking the time to honor the late actor. Also, a number celebrities have been honoring Stewart, including more than a few of his Star Trek cohorts. On that note, John de Lancie is now adding his voice to the many who've been sharing their memories of the Jean-Luc Picard portrayer. The beloved Q actor paid a fitting tribute to his former co-star and dropped the perfect reference tied to Picard and Q's past tussles.

While he wasn't a main character, John de Lancie's Q became one of Star Trek: The Next Generation's most memorable foes. After many adventures over the years, including Picard, De Lancie posted the following message about Stewart on Facebook:

For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard’s side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn. Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him. The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing. Goodbye, Patrick. You touched so many. See you out there, Mon Capitaine.

That "mon Capitaine" brought a tear to my eye when I read it, and reminded me of some of my favorite TNG episodes. While Q and Picard's relationship ran hot and cold, I could always sense that it was always love coming from the former's end. Of course, he was certainly a jerk, putting Picard through some wtf-worthy scenarios, but I always appreciated that there was some mutual love between them at the end of Picard's second season.

I'm A Star Trek Fan, But I'd Never Heard This Cool Story About Patrick Stewart Showing Up On Jeremy Clarkson's Set

For those who haven't streamed Picard Season 2 with a Paramount+ subscription, the storyline ends with Picard's realization that Q has constructed the entire scenario he's put them through in order to help him overcome past trauma. Q then reveals to Picard that he is dying, and the two share a hug before Q sets the timeline right again.

It was emotional for me, even if it was potentially retconned when Picard Season 3 had Q return in a post-credits scene. Fans have, however, theorized that everything from the Q species exists outside of time. Therefore, his death doesn't have to be linear.

Personally, I think Q is not above faking his own death just for the thrill of pulling one over on Picard. The fact of the matter is, we'll likely never know now that Patrick Stewart is gone, though I'm sure he won't be the last to play Picard. Star Trek hasn't been afraid to recast iconic characters, though I think it'll be a challenge for someone to follow in Stewart's footsteps and play the role.

Patrick Stewart's death comes amid the celebration of Star Trek's 60th anniversary, which has been rife with bad news. As far as the franchise itself goes, there is a movie in development, but no TV shows are actively in the works as far as the general public knows. Stewart's passing certainly feels like a gut punch to the fandom and the former actors, many of whom held out hope for positive news before the year's end.

Tributes continue to pour in for Patrick Stewart, and I'm continuing to love every eulogy and story that is shared. Both Star Trek: The Next Generation and Picard are available to stream on Paramount+, so anyone who is missing the great Captain should head over there and watch some classic episodes.

#3537. Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death Is a Documentary About the Shocking Deaths of Two Biohacking Influencers

If you’re familiar with the term “looksmaxxing,” which refers to an online trend dedicated to optimizing one’s life by way of physical improvement through steroids and peptides made popular in the manosphere, then you’ve inevitably come across Clavicular. The 20-year-old influencer, born Braden Peters, has become the (often bone-smashed) face of this male-dominated internet subculture. Famous for viral stunts that often leave him bruised, battered, or, in at least one instance, hospitalized, Peters has faced a slew of legal battles while documenting his physical transformation for his more than 2 million followers.

“It was actually never a Clavicular thing,” says director Stacey Lee, the filmmaker behind Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, a three-part docuseries about manosphere biohackers that begins streaming on Hulu November 10. News that the online looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular would appear in a documentary “got picked up and swept into places that weren’t what we were up to,” Lee tells Vanity Fair in her first interview about the project.

“Look, when you’re making a documentary about influencers, it’s very hard for the documentary itself not to become caught up in that [world],” she says, clarifying that Clavicular was never the documentary’s focus. “We were looking to spend time and actually understand these guys—not just as outrageous human beings, but what is driving them? Where are they coming from?” says Lee.

Following influencers like Clavicular may help illuminate what motivates an increasingly popular, exceedingly online idea of modern masculinity. A generation of boys who were socialized behind screens, and sold steroids as a cure-all for their societal woes, came of age in the two years that Lee and her crew spent shadowing various manosphere influencers, starting in 2023. “When we came in, this was niche,” says Lee, “and even after the first [day of] shooting, it was front and center, mainstream cultural conversation—politics, RFK, all these things coming into play as we were making this documentary. Simultaneously, all of the documentary’s main looksmaxxers “escaped to Thailand because America doesn’t offer them enough,” Lee says, shrugging. “So there’s a bit of contradiction in that.”

The resort city of Pattaya, Thailand, is where Lee was introduced to Tony Huge, born Anthony Hughes, an “overstuffed Marvel character,” a biohacking influencer who predated Andrew Tate, Bryan Johnson, and Clavicular, says Lee. “He became famous for taking DNP, which is a fat burner. Essentially you take one pill and lose a bunch of weight, you take two pills and…people [could] die,” she explains. “He was willing to go on camera and do things that a lot of people at the time were not. In the world of bodybuilding and fitness culture, so many men are taking a bunch of drugs but not really talking about it, whereas Tony took a different approach. And that created this brand, maybe an illusion for him, of radical transparency. But when you are like, you can see everything, it actually makes you more on guard like, what are we not seeing?”

Tony Huge, whose online mantra to his 250,000 followers across social media became “a day natty [short for natural] is a day wasted,” became a steroid-injecting pioneer for a group of vulnerable men, such as documentary participant Elon Muscular, a then-suicidal 19-year-old who messaged Hughes on Facebook and received an invite to his hero’s Thailand compound. “Young men were drawn into this world because they were disillusioned with the modern medical kind of environment of being told what not to do,” says Lee. “They were also feeling the statistics of loneliness and depression amongst men that are just becoming increasingly worse.”

Muscular found community in Hughes’s admittedly “cult-like” living situation, one where multiple men manipulated each other’s brain chemistry—and made social media content about it—all in the name of masculinity. “Most men come to Thailand because they’re mentally unstable,” Hughes says in the docuseries. Among his rotating circle of sidekicks was online influencer Leo Longevity, a fellow biohacker and self-described penis-enlargement expert who died in January 2023 inside the home that he shared with Hughes. (“Obviously, a penis influencer dying within this manospheric space was already a really absurd story,” says Lee. “But we started to see that this wasn’t just a one-off situation, but a larger reoccurring issue within this world, and certainly people that are part of this specific community. Then it became a little bit more urgent, the story.”

“Why Is Everyone Around Tony Huge Dying?” reads a YouTube comment under one of Hughes’s videos after the death of Longevity, real name Leif Abdallah Algaz, which is included in the documentary. That is a central question that also emerges in Looksmaxxing, as the series uncovers the string of sudden and strange deaths of Hughes’s closest confidants, including Nick Weisser (in 2018) and Josh Brooks (in 2021), and the apparent disappearance of Coach Trevor in 2022. “Throughout the process, I was very straight up with Tony, ‘I’m going to ask you all the things that everyone’s already talking about behind your back. And I think it’s really important that you have to answer them,’” Lee recalls. “He’s never fazed by that, to be honest, which doesn’t feel like a normal response. Tony said in the beginning, ‘I don’t care if I’m a villain or hero. I don’t know which one it is,’” says the director. “He gets censored so much that he’s just willing to put his story out and see.”

Lee’s crew began filming with Hughes following Algaz’s death. “Everyone was presenting a united front on camera, and behind the scenes there was a lot of conversation that we started to become aware of about how they were being portrayed or what they were going to say,” she says, even pitching ideas to the director. “Actually, no, that’s for your channel. Just be yourself and let’s see how that feels,” Lee told them. “These guys don't do therapy. We did offer them mental health services many times. But they exist in this matrix, so to speak. They don’t trust medical professionals, [preferring to rely on] their own best sense of judgment.”

Nevertheless, Lee was welcomed into Hughes’s scarcely female circle of trust. “I was in their life so much, it was like they forgot that I was a woman a lot of times. After we’d wrapped something, Tony would be like, ‘Oh, what did you think of that?’” she says. “It’s almost like he remembered that they were talking about Red Pill philosophy or whatever it was in front of me. I remember a conversation very early on talking about how women can’t be successful in careers and should never be a leader. And yet here I was, sitting here directing a team of mostly men in a documentary.”

Gender dynamics were harder to ignore when documenting the multiple women who live with Hughes in Thailand. “A man should only have as many girlfriends as he can leg press,” Hughes says in one video that’s in the docuseries. “In regards to the women, yeah, that was one of the hardest parts to witness,” says Lee. “That’s where the inherent contradiction of who he is comes in. He proposes freedom, yet he’s got these women that are forced to live with him. Well, they can leave at any point in time. But there’s power dynamics at play, money at play. He genuinely believes he’s helping, improving them. It’s a very complex situation to say the least,” the filmmaker continues. “It was important to give those women, where we could, the voice to speak for themselves, but also to showcase what biohacking looks like for them within that space.”

Lee and her crew also built trust with Hughes’s closest allies, including Connor Murphy, a fitness-influencer-meets-performance artist whose online presence was predicated on pranks and then, while living with Hughes, on being the influencer’s “art project,” Murphy says in the doc. “My parents are extremely worried because a lot of people in the atmosphere around you-know-who seem to be dying,” Murphy tells Lee in the documentary. “At first it frightened me, but now it kind of enlivens me. I almost feel like a wizard. The boy who lived—for now,” he adds, raising his eyebrows in a smirk.

“As we got to know the characters deeper, they weren’t just one lump unit, but their own tectonic plates that were constantly realigning,” says Lee. “And that’s symptomatic of the larger manosphere itself. Everyone’s climbing a totem pole. They were, in a way, competing over who gets to tell the story.”

Things came to a sudden halt on July 7, when Murphy died at the age of 32 in what authorities have ruled an apparent drowning. “Production had finished [four weeks earlier] when he passed. I was on the phone with these guys all the time talking to them about what’s going on and where they’re at,” says Lee, who grows visibly emotional at every mention of Murphy. “His death was absolutely shocking. When you spend two years filming with them and getting to know them just as a regular human being, it affected me deeply.”

Hughes subsequently made a video saying that Murphy drowned in his backyard lake during an erratic drug-induced episode. (Investigators reportedly found two unused syringes and several white pills in a bag inside Murphy’s car.) “His passing reinforced why we were making this documentary. He wasn’t just somebody who died,” says Lee. “Being able to show that complicated side of who he was and not just his death defining his life was really, really important for us.”

As the mother of a nine-year-old son, Lee worries about the dearth of positive male examples in online spaces. “With these influencers—the Tates, the Fuentes, all these guys who are performing masculinity, it was so apparent to me that we are lacking really good male role models, where men have each other’s backs, where they’re looking out for the best in each other, where they’re lifting one another up,” says Lee. The next generation of men are “looking at these guys and seeing it as a blueprint for their life. When you call yourself an influencer, there is a level of responsibility that needs to be taken for what you say and do,” she says. “And in this world, because they want to be anarchist and free and don’t take responsibility for anyone, that is what creates these tragedies.”

While more daring online personalities infiltrate the manosphere, “there is a sense of Tony losing relevancy,” Lee says of Hughes, who is father to three daughters and a son on the way with his live-in girlfriends. “When you lose relevancy,” she adds, “you try and control what’s closest to you. When your identity is built around pushing boundaries, what happens when the next generation’s going further than you? And how do you know when it’s enough?”

As the younger generation turns to new influencers in the biohacking space, Lee says there’s plenty of evidence to suggest looksmaxxers—and the appetite for their content—aren’t going anywhere. “What we are witnessing is nihilism within the next generation where it’s about living for today. I need to look as hot as I can today,” she tells VF. “We are being trained to find the easy, quick solution and those solutions are never going to fix these emotionally complex layers of confidence and purpose and true connection. Those aren’t going to be found online.”

#3535. Newly Confirmed DCU Batman Casting Detail Officially Rules Out 8 Fan Favorite Actors

James Gunn's DC Universe hasn't castBatman yet, but his criteria for Bruce Wayne's actor rule out some fan-favorite choices. Who will wear The Dark Knight's cowl in the rebooted DC franchise has been one of the biggest questions ever since Gunn and Peter Safran were put in charge of DC Studios. And while The Brave and the Bold has been in development nearly the whole time, they still need a Batman actor.

There have inevitably been plenty of fan-casts for who could be the DCU's Batman. Major stars have also expressed interest in taking on the iconic role, hoping to join Adam West, Michael Keaton, George Clooney, Val Kilmer, Christian Bale, Ben Affleck, and Robert Pattinson as live-action Batman actors. There's even been a huge push for Pattinson's The Batman franchise to merge with the DCU, but that idea has been squashed by all involved repeatedly.

Previous Batman actors have each brought a specific vision to life, and Gunn's DCU plans are starting to become clear. He recently confirmed it won't be long before Batman is cast, assuring that an actor isn't already signed on. But more importantly, Gunn specified that he wants Batman and Superman to be "around the same age," acknowledging that "they're future best pals."

Superman actor David Corenswet is 33 years old, which provides a rough idea to the age bracket Gunn is thinking of for Batman. He could be a little older, but probably by no more than 5 to 7 years. If Gunn's plan for Batman's age remains the same, we can go ahead and eliminate several actors who are popular fan choices.

There is perhaps no bit of DCU Batman fancasting more popular than Alan Ritchson. The Reacher star is an excellent action performer with an imposing frame, plenty of charisma, and an intensity that would pair well with The Dark Knight. Even though he has dismissed his own chances of playing Batman in the past, the confirmation of continued meetings with DC Studios has kept many hoping he'd get the role.

Ritchson might not look it, but he is 43 years old, making him 10 years older than Corenswet. He could play someone a bit younger than he actually is in real life and allow that gap to be reduced. However, it seems more likely that if Ritchson is going to play a third DC character (he's already played Aquaman in Smallville and Hawk and Titans), it will not be Batman.

Lee Pace has been another popular Batman casting suggestion. He's already connected to Gunn after playing Ronan the Accuser in Guardians of the Galaxy, but his screen presence is a big reason why so many have supported him. Notably, Pace refused to comment on Batman speculation last year, creating more hope that the Foundation star was in the running.

The issue for Pace is that he is 47 years old. He would certainly make for a great version of Batman who has been at this for years, but that doesn't appear to be the DCU's approach. The 14-year gap between Pace and Corenswet is too large for them to be considered similar ages, ruling him out.

Cavill may have already played Superman in the DC Extended Universe (and was booted from the role following Gunn and Safran's takeover), but several fans want to see him as Batman next. It's easy to envision him as Bruce in and out of the cowl. Gunn has even expressed an openness to find a new part in the DCU for the former Superman actor.

The actor has not shared similar interest in joining the DCU or taking on a different DC superhero role, and his chances of becoming Batman have now taken a hit. At 43 years old, Cavill is a full decade older than Corenswet. He often comes across as a bit more experienced than that, which wouldn't match Gunn's vision.

Barnes is one of the actors fans are on board with to be the DCU's Batman. He's a charismatic performer with an ability to go darker that would make him great in the role. Barnes confirmed his interest in Batman in 2025, saying he was "ready to go" and become Batman if Gunn wanted him.

Even if that was a thought for Gunn before, the newly confirmed age range for Batman cuts Barnes from consideration. He is 45 years old, making him 12 years older than Corenswet. That's too big of a gap for them to be considered around the same age.

On top of fans pushing Theo James for James Bond, he's also been a popular suggestion for Batman. His role in Netflix's The Gentlemen has shown more of his suave demeanor, and he's no stranger to major productions at this point. But at 41 years old and an 8-year age gap with Corenswet, he's likely just beyond Batman's desired age in the DCU.

This may come as a crushing blow to fans, but not to James. The actor distanced himself from this casting race in 2024, telling MovieDweeb, "I feel like there’s been about 70 Batmans. I feel like that’s pretty covered." The response makes it clear he wasn't gunning for the role then.

James has since said he wouldn't want to be Bond due to how it would change his life. Becoming Batman would do the same. For that reason, and his age, his name can stop being discussed.

In terms of actors linked to DCU's Batman casting rumors, Gyllenhaal is arguably the biggest and best actor of the bunch. He'd be a true movie star for the franchise to build around. He's got the perfect personality and range to differentiate Batman and Bruce, while still making it clear how they play off the other. And after Gyllenhaal missed out on Batman Begins, this would be a long-awaited opportunity for him.

The bad news for the actor is that he's already 45 years old, and he'll be 46 by the end of 2026. Gyllenhaal would be an excellent choice if Gunn wanted a slightly older actor as Batman, but he's hardly Corenswet's contemporary. Barring the DCU's plans changing or DC Studios' new owners at Skydance pressuring them to get a legit big name in the role, Gyllenhaal is out once again.

Jensen Ackles has been one of the most popular bits of DCU Batman fancasting from the beginning. The Supernatural, Tracker, and The Boys star has already proven he's a great Batman through voicing the character in animated projects, like Batman: The Long Halloween. His deep, brooding voice is an excellent fit for The Dark Knight.

Ackles' screen presence throughout his career shows he could be believable in live-action, too. Fans' hopes of this casting have been fueled throughout 2026, with Ackles confirming his interest in being the DCU's Batman.

At 48 years old, Ackles is one of the oldest actors fans have latched onto. But the 15-year age gap between him and Corenswet is too wide to make work with Gunn's vision. By the time the DCU's Batman debuts in live-action, Ackles will likely be over 50 years old, making it impossible for him to stay in the role as long as Gunn needs.

Gunn's idea for Batman's age in the DCU is another knock against Pattinson continuing on, too. The Batman's star is already 40 years old, and he'll be almost 42 by the time The Batman Part II comes out, even if he's playing a version of Bruce Wayne still in his early 30s. That does make the on-screen Batman about the same age as Corenswet's Superman, despite the actors' 7-year gap in real life.

Even if Pattinson and Corenswet were the same age, merging The Batman into the DCU would still be unlikely. Matt Reeves has a specific take on Batman and Gotham that he and Gunn want to keep separate. Pattinson has even continued to throw cold water on the idea, suggesting he wouldn't want to be Batman in as large a franchise as the DCU, even if he was age appropriate.
