#3534. 'Control Resonant' Becomes a Much-Needed Surprise Hit for Remedy

Resonant is Remedy's fastest-selling game ever

Fans of Alan Wake and Control creator Remedy Entertainment can finally breathe a sigh of relief. After executive shake-ups and fiscal underperformance at the beloved studio, it seems that the team’s latest game is finding an audience. In a new report released on Tuesday, Remedy wrote that Control Resonant “received excellent player reception and became the fastest-selling Remedy game to date.” The company's third-quarter revenue more than tripled compared to last year, surging by 226%.

What’s more impressive is that the revenue spike includes only Resonant’s pre-orders and its first seven days of sales before the end of the company’s third quarter in late September. The game was released on Sept. 24.

Remedy’s new CEO, Jean-Charles Gaudechon, was quite happy with the game’s performance. “This is our first self-published game of this scale, built on our own Control IP. Praised by players and critics alike, it marks a defining milestone for the company.” Back on Oct. 15, Remedy announced that Resonant had already sold one million copies.

Gaudechon went on to highlight how the game was praised for “Remedy’s willingness to take creative risks and surprise its players.” He added that he was happy with the game’s technical performance. "Positive commentary over its scalability across a variety of PC hardware meant a larger audience could enjoy Control Resonant. This is a testament to our in-house Northlight game engine, which enables the distinctive look and feel that has come to define Remedy’s games.” While Resonant didn't receive unanimous critical praise, reviews were generally positive, albeit not as glowing as the studio's usual output.

Resonant was clearly a big swing for the company, as Gaudechon added that the game received the studio’s largest marketing investment in its history. The United States was its largest market, accounting for nearly half of sales. On PC, China and the U.K. ranked second and third after the U.S., while the U.K. and Canada were second and third for console sales.

Gaudechon expressed satisfaction that the game reached a wider audience. “Based on analytic data, close to 50% of players were new to Control,” he said. “Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy.”

In June 2025, Remedy released the multiplayer game FBC: Firebreak, which received fairly tepid reviews and failed to find players. Remedy said the game didn’t meet sales expectations, prompting a profit warning that the company wouldn't hit its fiscal targets for the year. 12 days after the profit warning, former CEO Tero Virtala left his role. Remedy posted a €14.9 million operating loss for 2025.

On Feb. 9, 2026, the company announced that former Electronic Arts executive Gaudechon was the company’s new CEO. While there were concerns that the change would make Remedy resemble the much-hated EA, at least so far, that hasn’t happened. Hopefully, Control Resonant's success means the studio will remain a bastion of strange ideas in a game industry that's increasingly playing it safe.

#3531. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3530. The Original Witcher Officially Returns Next Month With New Release

The ORIGINAL Witcher is returning with a brand-new release this December. So if you're a fan of Geralt of Rivia at his best, you'll want to keep this release on your radar. It will remind you what made the character and world Andrzej Sapkowski created such a pop culture phenomenon in the first place.

Before Liam Hemsworth, there was Henry Cavill, and before Henry Cavill, there was Doug Cockle. Before Doug Cockle, there was Michał Żebrowski. In short, several men have brought Geralt of Rivia to life, whether through live-action performances or voice acting alone. However, before all these legends, there was Andrzej Sapkowski, the brilliant mind behind The Witcher. Now, Sapkowski’s original The Witcher is returning this December with a brand-new release that die-hard fans won't want to miss.

H.P. Lovecraft's horror masterpieces have inspired countless adaptations, but one of his most underrated stories is finally getting a new adaptation.

For those unfamiliar with the franchise's origins, The Witcher legacy began long before Netflix's live-action adaptation and even before the legendary video games. In fact, Geralt of Rivia first appeared in The Witcher (Wiedźmin), an original short story published in 1986. This was followed by several more short stories, eventually collected in Sword of Destiny and The Last Wish. The franchise then expanded into a Polish comic series before developing into the novels that fans know and love today: Blood of Elves, Time of Contempt, Baptism of Fire, The Tower of the Swallow, and The Lady of the Lake.

These books served as the source material and inspiration for what would eventually become a hit video game franchise and live-action TV series. Now, Andrzej Sapkowski's acclaimed short story collection The Last Wish is coming in a new format on December 15, 2026, giving fans the chance to experience this iconic collection like never before.

Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher: The Last Wish — The Complete Collection HC will hit comic book shelves this December, delivering a complete graphic novel adaptation of Sapkowski’s acclaimed short story collection in a prestigious oversized deluxe hardcover format. Fans should note that this is NOT simply a reprinting of previously published material. This edition will feature completely new cover art with foil stamping, silver foil-gilded edges, a cover gallery, a sketchbook section, and even a ribbon bookmark. But wait, there’s more!

In addition to collecting the six graphic novel adaptations of Sapkowski’s short stories, The Witcher, A Grain of Truth, The Lesser Evil, A Question of Price, The Edge of the World, and The Last Wish, this premium tome ties each story together with “the new, never-before-published adaptation of the framing story The Voice of Reason.” This is especially exciting, as it lets fans experience the classic collection in a way they haven't before.

Also notable is the fact that this hardcover edition will feature a foreword by internationally bestselling author Peter V. Brett (The Demon Cycle). This special edition arrives as part of Dark Horse’s celebration of the 40th anniversary of Sapkowski’s Wiedźmin, the story that started what has since become one of the dominant franchises in the dark fantasy genre. It's an exceptional journey, especially since the story first debuted in the Polish fantasy magazine Fantastyka and has since expanded to dominate gaming platforms, bookshelves worldwide, and Netflix.

For those who need a refresher on the type of story presented in The Witcher: The Last Wish--The Complete Collection HC, you can find Dark Horse’s official synopsis for the collection below:

Geralt is caught between violent feuds, beastly curses, and the confines of destiny in these tales of tragedy, passion, and bloodlust. Geralt sets out to claim a bounty on a bloodthirsty creature, but he is to cure the monstrosity, not slay it, for the creature is said to be retribution for the king’s dark secret. Next, Geralt encounters a beast with the faculties of man and discovers that within fairy tales, the truth is revealed.

Then, superstitions of an inborn evil pit a mage against a young woman, but with each committing acts of cruelty and carnage, who is the true evil? And fate plays a hand at a banquet to find a suitor for the princess when a mysterious guest ignites chaos within the royal family. In another story, Geralt and Dandelion search for a devil who they are to cast out, but not kill. Finally, witness Geralt and the sorceress Yennefer’s first encounter as they battle a djinn whose power lies beyond granting wishes.

#3528. A Christmas Horror Movie With A 0% On Rotten Tomatoes Flopped At The Box Office

A new horror comedy film has become both a rare critical disaster and a sizable box office flop. "Christmas at the Kringles" opened over Halloween weekend, though one would be forgiven for not noticing. For starters, Halloween fell on a Saturday which meant most people weren't going to the movies. For another, the weekend's new offerings were a bit lackluster, as evidenced by this newcomer from Briarcliff Entertainment.

"Christmas at the Kringles" opened to just $675,000 on 1,825 screens, giving it a terrible $369 per-screen average and landing it all the way down at number 17 on the charts. The film was directed by Kevin Lewis, the man behind the Nicolas Cage fighting killer animatronics movie "Willy's Wonderland," among others. He's not a terribly high-profile filmmaker, but this isn't going to help his case when it comes to his future.

Perhaps worse than the opening weekend number is the response from critics, as "Christmas at the Kringles" holds a rare 0% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. It's not that horror movies need critics on their side. The recent box office success of "Other Mommy" proved that horror is critic proof to some degree, but this is next level bad. A film like this was always going to lean on VOD and streaming, but the awful response is likely to turn away quite a few would-be viewers.

"Christmas at the Kringles" follows the Seversons as they start fresh in a quiet suburban neighborhood where their neighbors, the Kringles, celebrate Christmas year-round. But what begins as charming quickly turns unsettling, as the Seversons' concerns about their son's growing attachment to the family leads to lots of action-packed holiday chaos. The film's cast includes Ron Livingston ("Office Space"), Rachel Bilson ("The O.C."), Thomas Lennon ("Reno 911"), and Donald Faison ("Scrubs"), among others.

"Christmas at the Kringles" was a big creative swing, as Christmas horror comedy films aren't surefire slam dunks. But if this kind of thing works, it can extend well beyond the box office. To be certain, a Christmas flick can make its way into the annual rotation, meaning money indefinitely. But unless this one becomes an unlikely cult favorite, that's probably not going to pan out.

There are plenty of underrated Christmas horror movies out there. Even ones with a more comedic bend, such as "Krampus" or, most famously, "Gremlins," have found success. But this was a big swing and a bigger miss. The timing didn't help, either, as it's just a touch too early for people to get into the X-mas spirit, while movies like "Clayface" offered a better option for horror fans in theaters.

Briarcliff had reason to believe it might work out, too. "Terrifier 3" killed it at the box office in 2024, pulling in $90 million worldwide. Granted, that was after "Terrifier 2" became a surprise sensation. The "Terrifier" movies have also garnered surprising levels of critical praise, despite the hardcore gore on display.

Even last year's "Silent Night, Deadly Night" was a bloody remake with something new to offer. It wasn't a big hit, but it was received reasonably well. The larger point is that the Christmas horror genre is nothing new and has definitely led to success in recent years. On paper, this one could have worked. But in practice, it's a disaster in every way success is generally measured in Hollywood.

"Christmas at the Kringles" is in theaters now.

#3526. The Elder Scroll 6: Sentinel's Name Quietly Teases Juicy 'Skyrim' Sequel

A closer look at how TES6 might connect to Skyrim and The Elder Scrolls Online

Eight years after the original announcement, we've finally learned the name of Bethesda's next RPG: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Since the developer didn't show any gameplay footage, all fans can really do is muse on the meaning of the title. As disappointing as that is, Elder Scrolls loreheads do have plenty to chew on.

The subtitle has been an open secret for a while now — fans guessed it correctly years ahead of the reveal, and Xbox was teasing an eight-letter subtitle recently as well. The first and primary reason for this title should be obvious: it sounds cool. That's not the only reason, of course. Accompanying the title in the trailer was a short quote from Yazar, a Moth Priest serving High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell:

The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate.

The Hammerfell setting has been rumored for a while now as well, but the quote cements it in stone. Hammerfell is a region to the north of Skyrim, and it is the home of the Redguard race. Redguards are known for their strength, combat prowess, and resilience in harsh climates. Accordingly, Hammerfell and its deserts, jungles, and mountain ranges were once known as the Deathlands.

Hammerfell will be immediately recognizable to anyone who has played The Elder Scrolls Online. And the most consequential region in Hammerfell is arguably — drumroll please — Sentinel. Sentinel’s proximity to the sea makes it a critical trading post for Tamriel at large. Five major areas of Sentinel are already explorable in ESO: the docks, a Redguard gym, a grand royal palace, a massive open-air marketplace, and a sewer system.

Moth priests are a part of a cult that devotes itself to reading the actual Elder Scrolls. These priests use the scrolls to foretell the future in an effort to help monarchs like the Emperor or, in this case, the regional queen. The timing of the quote — 4E 206 — places Sentinel five years after the events of Skyrim.

It's worth knowing that Hammerfell has spent centuries embroiled between its northern and southern regions, but the area was unified by the time Skyrim takes place. That unification was primarily meant to help save Sentinel from an opportunistic Elven incursion that tried to take advantage of the ongoing larger turmoil.

A five-year time jump would likely further Hammerfell's era as a sovereign state — but that doesn't necessarily signal stability. Hammerfell's independence separates it from the larger empire that could provide it support during a time of need. That's important, because the elves probably aren't done with Hammerfell, either.

There are two primary events in Skyrim that are of note here. One involves the Dark Brotherhood quest where the player assassinates Emperor Titus Mede II. A death like that opens the door for the elves to launch an assault while the wider empire tries to pick up the pieces after the assassination.

The other quest, which involves a Redguard noble person named Saadia, is a perfect encapsulation of what players can expect in The Elder Scrolls 6. In it, Saadia claims she is being hunted by elves for speaking out. After the player investigates further, it turns out that Saadia actually betrayed the Redguard to help the elves. This sets a precedent that the elves have already infiltrated the highest echelons of power in Sentinel — and will probably find more ways to sow discord in the new game.

The quote is ambiguous but could be read as an attempt by Hammerfell's High Queen to figure out how to proceed in what is undoubtedly a messy situation.

Hopefully, Bethesda won't keep fans guessing for too long. It's been nearly a decade since the game was originally announced, and the RPG has apparently been playable since 2025. Fans are ready for something more than just a title screen.

'At this rate, The Elder Scrolls 6 will be less technically advanced than Skyrim by the time it comes out'

#3524. Avengers: Doomsday Ticket Presales Top Supergirl's Worldwide Box Office Run

Superhero movies have been experiencing troubled times of late. But "Avengers: Doomsday" might just be able to save the flailing genre. Thus far, the upcoming Marvel Cinematic Universe team-up movie has already set box office records with pre-sales, and now, it's just passed another significant milestone. According to a Forbes report from October 31, 2026, "Doomsday" took $125 million in pre-sales by the end of October across all cinema formats. This means that, by now, it has passed the entire box office gross for DC Studios' "Supergirl."

For the most part, DC Studios co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran have gotten off to a decent start with their DC Universe. The fledgling franchise has delivered such hits as the charming crowd-pleaser "Superman" and the HBO series "Lanterns," proving this latest cinematic enterprise can deliver everything from lighthearted superhero shenanigans to gritty comic book crime dramas. But there has been one glaring misstep thus far: "Supergirl."

Though the movie itself isn't actually all that bad (/Film's review noted that Milly Alcock shines as the self-destructive savior of the DCU in "Supergirl), its box office returns were less than heroic. Indeed, "Supergirl" took in just $126.5 million against a $170-186 million budget, which means "Doomsday" has now matched the film's entire gross before it's even hit theaters.

To be fair, that's more embarrassing for DC Studios than it is encouraging for Marvel Studios, as "Supergirl" isn't a major event movie featuring beloved characters that have been at the forefront of pop culture for the last 20 years. But while a movie that includes everything the MCU has to offer beating "Supergirl" at the box office in pre-sales alone isn't quite as big an accomplishment as it may seem, it's also a reminder that DC can't afford another "Supergirl"-level flop anytime soon.

Back in September 2026, "Avengers: Doomsday" set a major box office record for Marvel when it surpassed $50 million in pre-sales 100 days ahead of its release on December 18, 2026. That was good news for Marvel Studios and fans of the franchise, which has been conspicuously struggling in recent years as mass audiences tire of the interconnected superhero narratives being told by studio head Kevin Feige and his collaborators. As Forbes pointed out, however, "Doomsday" is far from a sure bet for the company.

According to the outlet, pre-sales are almost certainly coming from die-hard fans who want to secure their chance to see the movie as soon as it drops. But 2025's "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" also saw a solid turnout from die-hards before its box office took a hit. That said, it seems unlikely "Doomsday" will suffer a similar fate. Not only is this an Avengers movie, which carries a certain amount of prestige and recognition, Marvel Studios has packed this thing with fan-favorite characters a là 2024's "Deadpool & Wolverine" — which, as it happens, was a major box office success.

With Robert Downey Jr. set to make his MCU return as Victor Von Doom, alongside beloved MCU characters of the past and the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men, it seems likely "Doomsday" will succeed simply by sheer crowd-pleasing power. Meanwhile, there's no getting around the fact that "Supergirl" flopped hard at the box office earlier this year, and DC Studios will want to avoid any similar occurrences with its upcoming slate.

In light of how superhero movies have struggled in recent years, "Supergirl" seemed doomed from the outset. Taking lesser-known characters and turning them into cultural icons worked for Marvel Studios back in the late 2000s and 2010s after 2008's "Iron Man" became the unlikely superhero movie that changed Hollywood forever. But that started yielding diminishing returns by the 2020s, as audiences grew tired of having to keep up with wider developments in the shared universe via middling streaming series and bland, paint-by-numbers movies.

As such, James Gunn's decision to follow up "Superman" with "Supergirl" seemed sort of baffling. We'd seen Milly Alcock's Kryptonian show up briefly in "Superman," but otherwise, this was an unknown iteration of a second-tier DC character who quite clearly had very little box office pull at the time she was given an entire movie. Jason Momoa's Lobo was on-hand to try to increase the appeal, but it was obvious that mass audiences weren't going to turn out. With that in mind, it's not surprising that "Doomsday" has already surpassed the entire box office take of "Supergirl."

Now, the question becomes whether "Doomsday" can, in fact, overcome the issues highlighted by Forbes to establish itself as the true savior of the MCU. The original "Doomsday" teaser trailers were boring, frankly, and RDJ's return as Doctor Doom was met with confusion among fans who remain perplexed as to why the actor is playing a major Marvel villain rather than Tony Stark/Iron Man. But Marvel has clearly managed to increase the hype for this movie since those early days of "Doomsday" promotion. The film matching the box office for "Supergirl" is just the latest sign that things are headed in the right direction.

#3523. New Mistborn Movie Officially Gets Major Kelsier and Vin Casting Update

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Casting Mistborn means finding someone who can make overthrowing an immortal ruler sound like a reasonable use of an afternoon. Kelsier needs that kind of confidence. He’s recruiting a crew for an undertaking that should be impossible, and much of the fun of Brandon Sanderson’s first novel comes from watching him convince people to attempt it anyway. Whoever plays him has to make that enthusiasm infectious without sanding off his more dangerous edges.

Vin presents a different challenge. Her suspicion of other people is something she has earned, and accepting Kelsier’s help doesn’t instantly undo it. An adaptation needs audiences to invest in her gradual willingness to trust, alongside the considerable pleasure of watching her discover what she can do with Allomancy. Getting both characters right matters far more than assembling an impressive cast announcement.

Sanderson wants an established star to play Kelsier, while newer talent could take on Vin and Elend in Apple’s Mistborn movie. Discussing the adaptation during a Halloween livestream, the author outlined an approach that would give the project a recognizable leading name without requiring one for every major role. No actors have been announced for those parts, according to a report from Screen Rant. The comments describe what Sanderson hopes to achieve with casting, rather than negotiations with particular performers. He is currently working on the screenplay’s second draft following feedback from Apple. His official adaptation news page records the completion of the first draft in July, while emphasizing that it represents an early step in a much longer process.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

For audiences encountering this world for the first time, Kelsier is an effective introduction. He understands the society Vin is learning to navigate, has a plan for dismantling it, and possesses enough charisma to keep people listening when that plan sounds suicidal. A familiar actor could give viewers an immediate reason to follow him into an unfamiliar fantasy setting. There’s an equally appealing argument for letting audiences discover Vin alongside a less familiar performer. She is the story’s central perspective, and her transformation needs to feel like something happening to a person rather than another showcase for an established screen persona. That doesn’t require an unknown actress, but it makes finding the right fit more interesting than simply chasing the largest available name.

The movie adapts The Final Empire, which follows Vin as she joins Kelsier’s crew in a world dominated by the Lord Ruler. Its combination of a heist, a rebellion, and a carefully constructed magic system gives the adaptation plenty to accomplish before considering the wider Cosmere. Sanderson’s other major Apple project, The Stormlight Archive, is being developed for television. For now, readers can keep debating their ideal Kelsier. Sanderson has explained the kind of casting he wants; the name attached to it remains the part everyone is waiting for.

Mistborn does not yet have an announced release date.

#3522. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3521. The Gilded Age’s Replacement For George & Bertha Russell Is Already Perfect After 1 Episode

Warning: SPOILERS for The Gilded Age Season 1, Episode 1 - "Ring The Bells"

The Gilded Age season 4 premiere minted a new power couple that's already a perfect replacement for George (Morgan Spector) and Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon). The fourth season of The Gilded Age picks up about nine months after season 3's ending, when Oscar Van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) proposes forming "a fighting pair" with his old ally, Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran).

For the first three seasons of The Gilded Age, Bertha and George Russell reigned as the most powerful and the happiest marriage in New York society. The new money tycoon and his ambitious wife were equally ruthless; George's cut-throat tactics running Russell Industries were matched by Bertha's single-minded pursuit of ruling status over society's wealthy elite.

However, the tiny fissures in the Russells' marriage became seismic in The Gilded Age season 3. George was furious at Bertha for essentially selling their daughter, Gladys (Taissa Farmiga), to Hector, Duke of Buckingham (Ben Lamb), whom George also financially rescued. After George survived an assassination attempt, he separated from Bertha. They're still an ocean apart when The Gilded Age season 4 begins.

The Gilded Age season 4 kicked off with something Agnes Van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) feared she'd never live to see: her son Oscar getting married. Oscar and Enid officially became the new Mr. and Mrs. Van Rhijn. As they planned, it was a fusion of his family's name value and power in society with the wealth she inherited from her late husband. Oscar couldn't have asked for a better wife.

The Gilded Age returns for its fourth season with supreme confidence and a renewed focus on family drama and testing its huge cast of characters.

Mr. and Mrs. Van Rhijn were triumphant in The Gilded Age season 4's premiere, and Oscar and Enid are as much fun together as audiences hope. Oscar is a charmer, but Enid also knows how to play the game and win over their admirers. The Van Rhijns also threw a better party with a younger crowd in Webster Hall. Enid and Oscar are a welcome infusion of chaotic revelry in The Gilded Age.

Oscar and Enid aren't shy about gunning for the Russells and taking them down, having already heard about the cracks in George and Bertha's marriage. Just as Bertha dazzled society with posh dinners and extravagant balls, Oscar and Enid decided to make their own mark by throwing cutting-edge salons for society's youthful set, where they "can serve cocktails!" Oscar said excitedly.

With George Russell having found his would-be assassin, he still has no intention of living with Bertha, so their marriage doesn't look to be repaired any time soon. Meanwhile, Oscar and Enid bring youth and style to society. As a couple, they have the raw ambition that George and Bertha used to have together. In just one episode of The Gilded Age, the Van Rhijns became the happiest new power couple in New York.

It's early days for the new Mr. and Mrs. Van Rhijn, but thus far, their private arrangement seems to be working. Enid is fully aware that Oscar is gay, and wants to have dalliances at the lake house left to him by his dead former lover, John Adams (Claybourne Elder). Oscar has no intention of consummating his marriage to Enid.

There was a hint that the new Mrs. Van Rhijn may not always be satisfied with Oscar deferring his husbandly duties.

For her part, Enid indulges Oscar's sexual preference, and is fine with their marriage as is. However, at the end of The Gilded Age season 4's premiere, when the Van Rhijns retired to their separate rooms in Enid's palatial home, there was a hint that the new Mrs. Van Rhijn may not always be satisfied with Oscar deferring his husbandly duties.

Enid is still young and beautiful, and it's understandable if she wants a romantic partner of her own, especially if Oscar is free to pursue other men. If Enid chooses a lover, it could shift the balance of power in her marriage to Oscar, since he is bound to be jealous. There's also the question of what happens if Enid decides she wants a child, whether with Oscar or another man, who would inherit the Van Rhijn name.

Another wrench in Oscar and Enid's marriage could be Agnes Van Rhijn, who confronted her new daughter-in-law about being Turner, Bertha's lady's maid. Enid placated Agnes by promising to finance her dinner with President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan). While Oscar and Enid seemed charmed and on the ascent right now, the Van Rhijns' marriage could get bumpy as The Gilded Age season 4 continues.

#3520. One Of 2026's Best Anime Movies Is Based On The Same Book As A Tom Cruise Sci-Fi Classic

In Doug Liman's 2014 sci-fi action movie "Edge of Tomorrow," Tom Cruise plays William Cage, a cowardly public relations officer drafted to fight in the front line of an alien war. Dying due to exposure to an alien's acidic blood traps Cage in a time loop, and with help from decorated soldier Sergeant Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt), he has to find a way to break the loop and win the war. The movie did not perform especially well at the box office, grossing $381 million against a $178 million budget, but it earned good reviews and, to this day, fans and the creative team remain hopeful about an eventual "Edge of Tomorrow" sequel.

You might assume the nifty premise of "Edge of Tomorrow" is just an action movie riff on "Groundhog Day," but its real origins are more obscure. The movie adapts a 2004 Japanese light novel, "All You Need Is Kill," written by Hiroshi Sakurazaka with illustrations by Yoshitoshi Abe ("Serial Experiments Lain"). The movie and novel share a basic premise, though the movie moves the setting from Japan to Europe. It also turns the novel's hero, a young Japanese man named Keiji Kiriya, into Cruise's William Cage.

Fitting for a story that's all about its characters caught in a loop, "All You Need Is Kill" has been adapted several times. In 2014, Weekly Young Jump serialized a 17 chapter "All You Need Is Kill" manga written by Ryosuke Takeuchi and drawn by Takeshi Obata, artist of "Death Note." Most recently, Japanese studio Studio 4°C turned the story into a mostly 3D-animated film that opened in theaters this past year. The "All You Need Is Kill" anime does justice to the story while making some of the biggest changes to it yet.

The anime "All You Need Is Kill" retains the title of the novel, unlike "Edge of Tomorrow." ("Edge of Tomorrow" was originally titled "All You Need Is Kill," but was then renamed in 2013 ahead of release. Confusingly, it's also since been labeled as "Live Die Repeat" on home media.)

You might expect that the animated "All You Need Is Kill" is a more faithful adaptation, one that strives to tell the real story after Hollywood distorted it. But that's not quite true. While the animated movie retains the Japanese setting, it flips the story in another way: Rita Vrataski is the protagonist. In the novel and "Edge of Tomorrow," she's a soldier who got caught in a previous loop, escaped it, and walked out a hardened battlefield hero distinguished by her large war axe.

In the animated "All You Need Is Kill," we see her stumbling through loop after loop learning to fight. She's more like the novel's Keiji but with Rita's name, and then Keiji being caught in her same loop is the midpoint twist. The movie's ending also echoes "Edge of Tomorrow." The hero (William/Rita) breaks the loop, defeats the aliens, and arrives back at the beginning of the story (but now free of the loop). They then reunite with their partner (Rita/Keiji) with the hope they'll become close again.

The novel and manga's final twist is that, to escape the loop, one of Rita and Keiji has to die. Rita lets Keiji kill her, and he has to carry her sacrifice through to all his tomorrows. Therein lies the meaning of the title, "All You Need Is Kill."

In "Edge of Tomorrow," the soldiers fight with mechanical exoskeletons with guns directly attached to their forearms, while the alien "Mimics" resemble writhing, glowing masses of black tentacles. The manga has a similar aesthetic; Takeshi Obata draws the soldier's uniforms resembling Spartan armor from "Halo" (a vibe also seen in "Edge of Tomorrow" concept art), while the Mimics are also depicted as pure black orbs with large, toothy mouths.

The aesthetics of "All You Need Is Kill" are much stranger and more alien. Rita's armor more resembles an astronaut or a deep sea diver's suit, complete with a transparent bubble helmet. The limbs of the armor are also lanky and exaggerated, with digitigrade legs. The suit looks like it was designed for wider reach than a human can manage, but it doesn't scream "armored" or "intimidating" like the manga or "Edge of Tomorrow" suits do. The aliens are also even weirder, resembling giant, mobile flowers with bright purple-green color schemes.

In an interview with Animation Magazine, "All You Need Is Kill" director Kenichiro Akimoto explained he wanted to depict something a bit different than the "space marines blasting aliens" look of past iterations:

"I wanted to depict a colorful, vibrant hell. The thinking behind that was that this time loop repeats the cycle of life and death. Rita needs to live repeatedly, beautifully, as she faces this inevitable death. I wanted to send the message that life can be beautiful — that's the reason for the film's hypersaturated color palette."

The palette does indeed clash with past iterations' violence and brutality, resembling a landscape of imagination more than a warzone. But at its heart, "All You Need Is Kill" is a romance, and the movie's look grows out of that.

#3519. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3518. Overwatch Mid-Season 5 Patch Notes Released With Big Tweaks

Jetpack Cat is weaker, Doctrine's cooldowns are longer, and Illari gets some welcome buffs

The penultimate season of Blizzard's big Overwatch revamp is coming to a close in the next few weeks, and Blizzard's got quite a lot more hero tweaks than usual in the mid-season patch notes. Some of them are minor, prompted by this season's changes to projectile sizes. Reaper's a big guy and an easier target now, for example, so Blizzard's bumped up his base health. Meanwhile, Illari's primary fire charge finally gets dropped a bit, and her healing pylon pumps out a bit more health. It's not quite the full kit overhaul folks have been asking for in the last few months, but it's a start.

We've rounded up all the Overwatch season 5 mid-season patch notes below.

There's a large selection of other small-but-important tweaks, too. Ana's biotic grenade is less potent (again), D.Mon has to commit to her shield and can't just pop it out for a split second save anymore, and Anran's primary fire gets a much-needed buff so she can do more than just fan the flames. There's nothing on the level of nerfing Cassidy's High Noon like Blizzard did at the start of the season, but the tweaks are still substantial enough that you'll notice the change the next time you play.

If you thought Mauga dropped off the face of the game over the last few weeks, you weren't wrong. Blizzard said Mauga's past tweaks reduced his effectiveness, so now he's getting some of his armor back and burns opponents more effectively.

Winston was healing far too much with his barrier perk. Now he still heals a lot — just slightly less.

Anran's getting tweaked quite a bit. In addition to her primary fire buff, her ultimate cast time is slightly faster now. And you can't spam her "Inferno Rush" perk to drop that skill's cooldown time so dramatically anymore. It only counts the first time you hit a target.

Blizzard still hasn't landed on the right place for Emre, but it's getting closer.

Sombra's position as supreme hacker is no longer in question. Sorry, Hanzo.

I'm glad I wasn't the only one to think Shion's ultimate timing felt harder to nail down than it should be. Blizzard's reducing it slightly and dropping the initial spread for "Execution" so you can do higher damage at close range without a full charge.

It's been a year, and Vendetta's still giving Blizzard trouble. This time, the solution is to slow her down and tweak her Whirlwind Dash perk — good news for anyone tired of getting bounced into the walls repeatedly by it.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

In the spirit of helpful UI additions, you can now see who actually benefits from Baptiste's area-wide healing skill.

Doctrine's overperformed a bit in his debut season, so now he's getting a small set of nerfs — longer cooldowns for his mobility skill and for infusion.

Playing against Jetpack Cat is equivalent to shooting a gnat with a rifle. So, Blizzard decided to nerf her health in a bid to balance any engagement she happens to zoom into. The trade-off is that Frenetic Flight is faster (again), but recovers fuel more slowly.

#3517. Idris Elba Almost Played A Different DC Comics Villain In James Gunn's The Suicide Squad

If you're a DC Comics fan, then "The Suicide Squad" casting Idris Elba as Bloodsport and using the character as the leader of the titular team was eyebrow-raising. Bloodsport had no previous association with the Suicide Squad, instead being a minor Superman villain distinguished by using Kryptonite bullets (which gets a brief nod in "The Suicide Squad" as part of Bloodsport's rap sheet).

It makes a lot more sense when you know the behind-the-scenes context. Will Smith, who played Deadshot in 2016's "Suicide Squad," wasn't available to return. So, Elba/Bloodsport took Deadshot's role in the movie. Initial reporting in 2019 even suggested Deadshot had been recast with Elba in "The Suicide Squad." But according to Elba himself, neither he nor director James Gunn wanted to replace Smith or his take on Deadshot. But Bloodsport still functions as essentially a renamed Deadshot. He even has a young daughter, Tyla (Storm Reid), who was clearly meant to be Deadshot's daughter, Zoe Lawton, at some point.

"The Suicide Squad" was made as part of the now-dead DC Extended Universe. With Gunn having since taken over as the co-head of DC Studios and rebooted the franchise via the DC Universe, the movie sits in a limbo of canon. Addressing the issue head-on, DC has now released a one-shot podcast — "The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon?" — featuring Gunn plus actors Jennifer Holland and Steve Agee discussing that exact question.

On said podcast, Gunn discussed how he got from Deadshot to Bloodsport. The change was at Elba's request, with Gunn saying Elba may have seen some "negative reaction" to him replacing Smith. Before settling on Bloodsport, though, Gunn considered having Elba play DC's most infamous mercenary character — Slade Wilson/Deathstroke — as the Squad's leader. Indeed, some "The Suicide Squad" concept art shows Deathstroke leading the team.

According to James Gunn, he decided against using Deathstroke in "The Suicide Squad" at the request of his actor friend Joe Manganiello, who had been previously cast as Deathstroke in the DCEU. Manganiello appears briefly as Slade in a post-credits scene for "Justice League," which was meant to set up Deathstroke as the main villain of Ben Affleck's never-made "Batman" movie. Casting Idris Elba as Slade would've certainly precluded Manganiello from playing Deathstroke again. So, as a favor to a buddy, Gunn dropped the idea of using Slade. Thus, with Deadshot and Deathstroke off the table, he eventually settled on using Bloodsport.

"I like Bloodsport so much. I'd like to see the character return," Gunn said on the podcast. "I also like working with Idris. Idris is a good guy, so I would like to see him return as Bloodsport or even somebody else."

That's definitely not a door closing, but it also sounds like DC Studios doesn't have any active plans to reuse Elba's Bloodsport right now. But one character who DC Studios is focusing on? Deathstroke! In 2024, it was reported that the studio was developing a team-up movie featuring Deathstroke and the infamous Batman villain Bane. As of October 2026, it's been reported that the project (titled "Savage Hunters") is a priority for DC Studios.

(Not for nothing, DC Studios is reportedly working on a "Teen Titans" movie as well. If that goes forward, maybe we can finally get Deathstroke in a film based on the comic where his character originated.)

Should we expect Manganiello to appear as Deathstroke opposite Bane? Not likely. Speaking with ComicBook.com in 2024, Manganiello said that Gunn advised him to "let it go," with "it" being the plans Manganiello had for Deathstroke.

#3516. An Unlikely Frasier Episode Earned Death Threats For Daphne Actor Jane Leeves

The "Frasier" revival probably should have been a one-off special, but  we'll always have 11 seasons of classic comfort sitcom hilarity regardless. "Frasier" ran from 1993 to 2004, maintaining a remarkable consistency over the course of 264 episodes. Kelsey Grammer's lovably snooty Dr. Frasier Crane and his family, friends, and co-workers will remain beloved by a generation raised on the NBC sitcom — unless, that is, you're oddly offended by cruelty against rubber eels. Yes, as Daphne Moon actor Jane Leeves reveals in her book "Daphne & Me: My Life on Frasier (And a Bit More)," her character whacking a rubber eel against a countertop earned her death threats from enraged viewers.

"The Innkeepers" is a fondly remembered episode from "Frasier" Season 2 in which the titular psychiatrist and his brother Niles Crane (David Hyde Pierce) decide to take over a failing restaurant and restore it to glory. Of course, nothing goes to plan, and the boys end up enduring an opening night from hell wherein their family and friends are all recruited to help keep the restaurant running as things fall apart in dramatic fashion.

"Frasier" had already ventured into farce with Season 2's "The Matchmaker." But "The Innkeepers" stands as a farcical triumph — despite, as Leeves points out in her book, some viewers believing it strayed too far from the show's otherwise sophisticated humor. But for other fans of the show, it wasn't the shift of comedic styles that was at issue. Instead, it seems Daphne's treatment of an eel in the kitchen of Les Frères Heureux (The Happy Brothers, as Niles and Frasier christen their culinary venture) was a crime worthy of death.

"The Innkeepers" single-handedly makes Season 2 one of the best seasons of "Frasier." In the episode, as a harried evening in Les Frères Heureux becomes even more fraught, Niles Crane — conscripted to chef duty alongside Daphne Moon — tries to bludgeon a tank of eels so as to not have to handle one of the live creatures. Meanwhile, Daphne's patience wears out. "Oh, for heaven's sakes," she exclaims before marching over to the tank, yanking out an eel, and slamming its head on the countertop. She then hands the lifeless fish to a stunned Niles in one of the episode's many moments of broad slapstick humor.

Turns out, it wasn't just Niles who was stunned. In "Daphne and Me," Jane Leeves reveals that she received threatening letters wishing her a torturous death for this transgression. "What I could never have anticipated were the death threats," she writes. "Yep, you heard me. I got death threats for my mistreatment of the clearly rubber eel. As explained in the scene-opening title card, 'No eels were harmed during the making of this episode.'"

Granted, Daphne gave the thing a good whack, and whoever was in charge of providing the rubber eel certainly delivered a fake fish with some convincing heft to it. But as Leeves goes on to point out, her killing the pretend fish was hardly the most egregious example of small screen violence. "At the time, shows like 'NYPD Blue' and many crime procedurals of the present day got away with, or even overtly endorsed, so much unconscionable carnage and brutality," she writes. "I wonder if they ever got letters?" Just in case you doubt the maliciousness of these missives, Leeves goes on to provide an example.

It might sound unbelievable that Jane Leeves received letters wishing her a painful death simply for clocking a rubber eel with a wooden counter. But in her book, the actor actually provides the text of one such letter. "Miss Leeves," it begins. "Every time I see the 'Frasier' episode where you smash the eel's head for a laugh I wish you'd get an agonizing terminal disease. It doesn't matter if the eel is real or fake. It ain't funny. I pray that you get smashed on the head, too." Bearing in mind this was long before the internet age, which means somebody had to sit down, write the letter, find the correct address, then mail it out. Maybe we were doomed before the internet subsumed our lives after all.

Interestingly enough, "The Innkeepers" was a moderately controversial episode of "Frasier" when it first aired. The show itself had debuted to stellar reviews and outstanding ratings. David Hyde Pierce might have felt the "Frasier" pilot was "terrible" at first, but the series premiere earned Emmy wins for Kelsey Grammer, writers David Angell, Peter Casey, and David Lee, and director James Burrows.

"The Innkeepers," however, prompted what Leeves called "mixed reactions." As the actor writes, "Some thought it strayed from the refined, sophisticated humor that was 'Frasier.' I disagree wholeheartedly. In my mind, 'Frasier' was one of the only shows capable of pulling off an ambitious, expertly-written slapstick comedy with such flair and sophistication, adding another tantalizing flavor to the show." Of course, now "The Innkeepers" is recognized for everything Leeves highlights — though whoever wrote her that letter probably never came around to it.

After the Marshals track down his accomplice, Derek McCoy, Kayce chases Derek's brother, Will McCoy (Keean Johnson), into a barn that collapses, trapping the pair below ground. It's here that Kayce decides to bring up his family and once again tease audiences with a crossover that is yet to materialize.

In "Secret Weapon," after the barn floor collapses, Will McCoy's leg is badly injured. While trying to find a way out of their predicament, Kayce tries to convince Will to give up details about his brother, who evidently treats Will like a "punching bag." Kayce takes the opportunity to talk about his own brother, Jamie Dutton (played by Wes Bentley on "Yellowstone), and his sister, Beth Dutton, who also treated Jamie like a punching bag. Of course, Beth ultimately kills Jamie Dutton in the final season of "Yellowstone," but Kayce stops short of mentioning that still buried crime.

"You remind me of my middle brother," he tells Will. "Never quite fit in, always on the bad end of a beatdown. My sister made his life hell." Will replies with antagonism. "Picked on by his sister? I'm not that pathetic." But as Kayce quite rightfully points out, "She'd eat you for lunch," adding, "Meaner than any of your brothers, guaranteed."

It's true that Beth Dutton is a force of nature, and that only makes it even more frustrating that she hasn't shown up in "Marshals," which could do with a jolt of energy at this point. Beth and Rip are too busy setting up shop in Rio Paloma, Texas, in the far superior "Dutton Ranch." But this brief mention of Kayce's sister and how she'd eat Will for lunch is a reminder of just how good we once had it with "Yellowstone," and how much "Marshals" is struggling to match the excitement of its predecessor. Of course, "Yellowstone" lost its way at one point, but Beth was never anything less than electrifying, and "Marshals" would benefit from having anyone in its cast with half as much charisma.

For now, these brief references in "Marshals" to beloved "Yellowstone" characters aren't doing the CBS procedural any favors. In "Secret Weapon," Kayce Dutton recalls how fighting wasn't in Jamie Dutton's nature. "He had to be smarter, more cunning," he says, "And eventually he broke from the family, forged his own path." Of course, that path ultimately ended in his death, with Beth taking a knife to the middle Dutton brother's stomach and exacting revenge for the controversial death of Kevin Costner's John Dutton earlier in "Yellowstone" Season 5.

The thing is, being reminded of the "Yellowstone" years is bad enough on a show that clearly struggles to match the quality of Taylor Sheridan's original neo-Western. But when you take into account the anticipation for a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, it's just downright frustrating.

The "Marshals" Season 1 finale seemed to set up a perfect crossover with "Dutton Ranch," but in the end we got nothing of the sort. We could still see Beth show up later in the season, but for now all we know is that another "Yellowstone" fan-favorite character will be appearing in "Marshals" when Jefferson White's Jimmy Hurdstrom makes his return to the Montana plains. In the meantime, let's hope the show finds a way to keep the "Yellowstone" connection alive without reminding us of what we're missing out on.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3513. Cillian Murphy's Overlooked 2024 Drama With A 94% Rotten Tomatoes Score Is A Must-Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Many of Cillian Murphy's best characters are either American, like J. Robert Oppenheimer or Jonathan Crane, or British, like Jim from "28 Weeks Later" or the immortal (?) Thomas Shelby from "Peaky Blinders." But as Murphy himself will remind you, he's Irish, and one of his most recent films tackles a dark part of his country's history.

That would be 2024's "Small Things Like These" by "Peaky Blinders" Season 3 director Tim Mielants, adapted from author Claire Keegan's 2021 novella. The movie received strong reviews and more than made its modest $3 million budget back with a $15 million gross in theaters, but it's still under-discussed. Sadly, that makes sense, as it's a quiet character study not really designed for a wide audience.

Murphy (who produced the film) plays Bill Furlong, a coal merchant in the Irish town New Ross during the 1980s. He's a moderately successful man, with his own business plus a wife and five daughters. But he remains troubled by his childhood, having been born out of wedlock and never known his father. If not for the kindness of his mother's employer, the widowed Mrs. Wilson (Michelle Fairley), who sheltered Bill and his mother, Sarah (Agnes O'Casey), like her own family, Bill would've likely been put up for adoption and Sarah sentenced to a Magdalene Laundry. What's that?

Until 1996, the Catholic Church in Ireland operated "Magdalene Asylums" for "fallen women" (unmarried women caught having sex or becoming pregnant, even if through sexual assault). These women were put to work to cleanse their supposed sins and basically enslaved. One of these laundries exists in Bill's own town, where everyone keeps their head down and doesn't peek too closely. But Bill, knowing he only has the life he does because of charity, can't look the other way.

Spoilers for "Small Things Like These" ahead.

In the opening shots of "Small Things Like These," church buildings loom over New Ross as their bells ring out. The Church's power is baked into the town and personified by the convent's Mother Superior (Emily Watson). Watson plays the soft-spoken nun as being so powerful that she doesn't have to be loud. Bill can't even meet her gaze as she makes subtle threats behind her niceties.

Bill's work in coal means that he comes home and cleans his hands every night, i.e. exactly the spiritually symbolic labor that the "fallen women" of the laundries are tasked to do. But a small kindness cleans Bill's hands: He saves an imprisoned girl locked in a shed, wrapping her in a coat and taking her to his home. Bill is particularly suited to break this social norm because of his background. The girl Bill saves, Sarah Redmond (Zara Devlin), literally has the same name as his late mother. As Bill walks with Sarah through New Ross, everyone around them looks on in shock and judgment. Yet, they're all out of focus, as if Bill is finally tuning them out.

"The fact was that he would pay for [taking Sarah], but never once in his whole and unremarkable life had he known happiness akin to this," reads one of the novel's closing lines. Speaking to GQ in 2024, Cillian Murphy even said Bill saving Sarah is "not a classically heroic act."

"Small Things Like These" came about in part due to Murphy's work on "Oppenheimer" and not just via his post-Oscar win clout. During that production, Murphy passed along the script to his co-star Matt Damon, who had recently founded the new studio Artists Equity with Ben Affleck.

"[Artists Equity] really let us make the film we wanted to make, because they're filmmakers themselves and writers, and they really understand it," Cillian Murphy told GQ. Indeed, "Small Things Like These" is extremely faithful to its somber source book and trusts its audience to weather the slow pace with Murphy's quiet but steely performance as an anchor.

Actor Eileen Walsh plays Bill's wife, Eileen Furlong, who advises him: "If you want to get on in this life, there are things you have to ignore." Walsh's casting rings hard because she previously appeared in Peter Mullan's 2002 film "The Magdalene Sisters" as Crispina, a woman imprisoned in one of those laundries. One of the greatest Irish films of the 21st Century, "The Magdalene Sisters" brought new attention to the real-life atrocities of the Magdalene Laundries (and was unsurprisingly condemned by the Catholic Church).

That "national reckoning" continues to this day, Murphy told GQ. "There's government commissions and government reports and academic papers on all of these things that you can get your hands on, but the public doesn't really read them. They will consume books and films, and I think it's a gentler way to confront it," he added. After all, "Small Things Like These" has as realistic a happy ending as one could hope for in this story.

In December 2024, shortly after the movie's theatrical release, the "Small Things Like These" novel was selected by Oprah's Book Club. That publicity is another win for civil education about the real history the novel dramatizes, at least the "gentler way." The book is only about 120 pages, and like the movie, it's easy enough to absorb in a single sitting if you set your stomach right for the cruelty inside.

Aaron Sorkin has spent decades writing some of the most celebrated movies and television shows in Hollywood, but it's fair to say his work as a director has never quite hit the same heights, and that is sadly the case once more with his sequel to The Social Network. Sony Pictures' The Social Reckoning, the follow-up to The Social Network, has officially ended its theatrical run after opening in 2,606 domestic theaters on October 9, 2026. The film stars Mikey Madison (Anora) as Frances Haugen, Jeremy Allen White (The Bear) as Jeff Horwitz, Jeremy Strong (Succession) as Mark Zuckerberg, Wunmi Mosaku (Loki) as Raya Akinola, Betty Gilpin (GLOW) as Christina, Billy Magnussen (Game Night) as Teddy Marks, Bill Burr (The Mandalorian) as Charlie Garrigan, Portia Doubleday (Mr. Robot) as Kaylee, Anna Lambe (True Detective: Night Country) as Morgan, Gbenga Akinnagbe (The Wire) as Andy, and Patrick Fischler (Mad Men) as Robbie.

The original movie starred Jesse Eisenberg (Zombieland) as Mark Zuckerberg, Andrew Garfield (The Amazing Spider-Man) as Eduardo Saverin, Justin Timberlake (Friends with Benefits) as Sean Parker, Armie Hammer (The Man from U.N.C.L.E.) as Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, and Rooney Mara (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo) as Erica Albright.
