#3510. The Martian Author Andy Weir Explains The One Thing He Would Change About The Story [Exclusive]

Looking back at the success of 2015's "The Martian," it's remarkable to realize just how influential this crowd-pleasing blockbuster really was. It helped launch author Andy Weir to the upper echelon of sci-fi writers, paving the way for even bigger box office hits like 2026's "Project Hail Mary." Alongside Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" in 2014 and Alfonso Cuarón's "Gravity" the year before, Ridley Scott's adaptation also served as a bellwether for the mid-2010s "space race" in film. And, for those of a certain age, there's something genuinely nostalgic about the tone struck by both the source material and the movie — a last gasp of the sense of optimism and unity that defined the Obama-era U.S.

So, when I had the chance to speak with Weir over a Zoom interview, as he's promoting his newest original project as an executive producer on Audible's "Exoplanet" series (due later this month), I jumped at the chance to revisit the whirlwind experience of "The Martian." Has over a decade of hindsight given Weir a different perspective on his game-changing book, now that he's more established as a novelist? In response, the science-abiding author maintained he wouldn't change anything ... except for the natural disaster that sets the plot in motion in the first place on the surface of Mars:

"If I had it to do over again, there's a few minor changes I'd make. I'd probably make the initial problem not be a windstorm, because that windstorm was not physics-accurate. I'd probably have it be — well, I've since learned that there's lightning strikes on Mars, and that could be something. Lightning strikes something, it causes overload here, that causes an explosion there, and then [the other astronauts have] all got to bail, something like that."

When things just happen to fall into place perfectly, you count your blessings and don't look back. That's more or less the mindset Andy Weir has with "The Martian." Unlike his hands-on role with "Project Hail Mary," Weir notes in our conversation, he was much more of a passenger on this first adaptation of his work. As a result, he simply sat back and let director Ridley Scott and screenwriter Drew Goddard do their thing along with some of the best and most talented actors in the world.

Sure, the part of his brain obsessed with making things as realistic and scientifically-accurate as can be may have some corrections or two. In the book, everything goes haywire when astronaut Mark Watney is separated from his fellow crew during a hellish windstorm and is left behind on the surface of Mars, presumed dead. But while there are dust storms on the surface of Mars, Weir is correct to note that the atmosphere and gravity of the planet couldn't sustain one of this magnitude. "But other than that," he tells me, "I don't think I'd change anything."

He goes on to compare the success of "The Martian" to, well, I'll let Weir's quirky sense of humor speak for itself:

"It's like, have you ever been casually talking to a beautiful woman and then you realize she's interested in you, and you have no idea what you did right, but you don't want to jinx it? That's kind of what happened to me with 'The Martian.' I'm like, 'I don't know what I did right, but I'm sure as hell not going to change anything.' [laughs]"

For those interested in more sci-fi approved by Weir, "Exoplanet" hits Audible on November 5, 2026.

#3509. 50 Years Ago Today: John Carpenter Directed A Gritty Action Thriller That Became A Cult Classic

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Retired filmmaker John Carpenter is best known for his horror films. After all, we don't have the modern slasher film without "Halloween." But before Michael Myers returned to Haddonfield on Halloween night 1978, Carpenter tried his hand at an action-exploitation film: 1976's "Assault on Precinct 13," which opened in theaters 50 years ago today.

Carpenter was born in 1948, the perfect age to grow up on cowboy movies. He dreamed of going to Hollywood to make Westerns, not horror films. But, by the time he enrolled in University of South California film school in 1968, Westerns had already faded as Hollywood's biggest genre. Throughout his decades-long filmmaking career, Carpenter never directed a Western — but you can see that longing in "Assault on Precinct 13." The movie has a courageous lawman who has to hold his ground against the black hat gangs. The catch? The movie is set in contemporary Los Angeles, not the Wild West.

Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is overseeing the closure of the LAPD's Precinct 13. A prison bus, carrying convicted murderer Napoleon Wilson (Darwin Joston), also stops at the precinct for a respite. Before long, the building is under siege by bloodthirsty gang members. Bishop, Wilson, and surviving secretary Leigh (Laurie Zimmer) are in a literal fight for their lives as unlikely allies.

Made on a meager budget of $100,000, "Assault on Precinct 13" wasn't an instant mega-hit. Reviews weren't too enthusiastic either. Whitney Williams of Variety was ambivalent, writing backhanded praise like, "some exciting action in second half packs enough interest to keep this entry alive for the violence market." Ellen Edwards of The Miami Herald condemned the film for its "hideous, unmotivated violence." But "Assault on Precinct 13" found its audience. It even got a remake in 2005, starring Laurence Fishburne and Ethan Hawke.

One of John Carpenter's acknowledged influences for "Assault on Precinct 13" is one of the most beloved Westerns ever: Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," about a sheriff (John Wayne) and his deputies trying to keep a murderer with a rich brother and many hired guns locked up. But "Rio Bravo" is not a tense thriller; often called a hangout movie, it's leisurely paced with only bursts of gun violence.

In "Assault on Precinct 13," the threat is everywhere. There's not even a reason for the siege beyond violence for its own sake; there's nothing of value inside the precinct besides more lives to end. That leads into one of the other movies that inspired Carpenter: George Romero's 1968 "Night of the Living Dead," the first modern zombie movie. When asked if "Night of the Living Dead" inspired "Assault on Precinct 13," Carpenter said, half-seriously, "Everybody who made a low-budget film was inspired by ['Night of the Living Dead']."

The comparison rings even more true here. Both movies are about people trapped inside a small building, surrounded by a horde outside that wants to break in and kill them. Both films also cast a Black man as their hero: Stoker as Lt. Bishop in "Precinct 13" and Duane Jones as Ben in "Night of the Living Dead." That was a bigger deal in the 1960s and '70s than it is now, and one spot where Carpenter's exploitation movie is rather progressive. "Living Dead" ends on a famously cynical note, with Ben shot by white men who mistook him as a threat. In "Precinct 13," Bishop and Napoleon Wilson achieve mutual respect; at the end of the movie, they walk out of the basement together as equals.

After its U.S. theatrical release in 1976, "Assault on Precinct 13" played along the European festival circuit, including the Cannes Film Festival and the London Film Festival. (At the latter, it received "deafening applause" per a contemporary review by The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.) Seeing the movie at Cannes, George Romero paid forward the compliment of Carpenter modeling his movie after "Night of the Living Dead."

The most shocking scene in "Assault on Precinct 13" is when a little girl, Kathy (future reality TV star Kim Richards), is shot in the chest after buying an ice cream cone. It's a jaw-dropping scene, and the movie is clearly having perverse fun turning such a taboo of violence against children into a spectacle and sick joke.

Quoted in Jason Zinoman's "Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood, and Invented Modern Horror," Romero testified to this scene's impact: "John Carpenter at Cannes wiped us off the face of the earth with 'Precinct 13.' Right from the scene when the little girl gets blown away, I was blown away." (The same book reports that, to get an R instead of an X rating, Carpenter cut the girl's death from the rating review board then added it back in before the film went to theaters.)

This sort of gang violence is echoed in Carpenter's later "Escape From New York," which is all about a future where the gangs like those in "Precinct 13" have taken over the Big Apple. Like "Escape from New York" and many of his other movies, Carpenter also composed the score for "Precinct 13." The title sequence theme, a synthesized anthem of droning dread, is still the most perfect mood setter for an action thriller even 50 years later.

#3508. Marshals Season 2 Episode 5 Exposes A Major Problem With The Yellowstone Spin-Off

"Marshals" Season 2 Episode 4 ended on a deadly cliffhanger that left the fate of Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz unclear. Caught in an explosion, the pair were flung through the air just before the episode cut to black. What would become of Kayce and the character with whom he's clearly developing deep feelings? Well, nothing. The latest "Marshals" installment quickly establishes that they were both fine in what is the latest example of one of the show's most frustrating problems.

It's no secret that Grimes' procedural has struggled to live up to "Yellowstone" and its fellow spin-off "Dutton Ranch." There are many reasons why. For one, "Marshals" Season 1 had no idea what it was about, with the show jumping from premise to premise in an attempt to find its footing and ultimately never succeeding. But there are several other issues with this show, and one of them is its proclivity for building things up only to disappoint viewers in the most unnecessary ways.

Consider the Season 2 premiere. "Marshals" Season 1 ended by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton taken captive by investor turned rancher Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey). Tate was supposedly being shuttled to Texas, where it seemed we might get the first official crossover between "Dutton Ranch" and "Marshals." But in the Season 2 premiere we learned that Tate was having a grand old time fishing on a Wyoming ranch. By the end of the episode, Tom Weaver had been apprehended and Tate was back to barely featuring in the series. Now, we've had yet another cliffhanger undermined and it's starting to get ridiculous.

"Marshals" Season 1 seemed to introduce a love triangle between Kayce Dutton, Andrea Cruz, and Dolly Weaver (Ellyn Jameson). Now that Dolly's out of the picture, however (she died in that disappointing "Marshals" Season 2 premiere), Andrea and Kayce are free to embrace their attraction.

Season 2, Episode 4, "Blast Radius," saw the pair growing closer than ever. Turns out this duo have been executing warrants as an extra-curricular activity to distract them from their sleepless nights. But it's clear there's also a slow-burn romance developing between the two. As such, when they were seemingly blown sky high in the episode's closing moments it looked as though the writers were about to leverage this burgeoning love affair for some dramatic tension. There was no way Kayce was going to die, but perhaps his new love interest's life would be left hanging in the balance?

Nope, they're both fine. Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" opens in the immediate aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding his bomb in range of Kayce and Andrea. We see the former lying unconscious on the floor, before he wakes up and crawls over to Andrea, who's also coming to. Meanwhile, their fellow Marshals do a sweep of the barn, determine Rudy's gone for good, and after that everything's back to normal. It's a frustrating opening as it calls to mind all the previous "Marshals" cliffhanger moments that have similarly come to nothing.

"Marshals" is a CBS procedural in the vein of "SEAL Team" — the show from which its showrunner Spencer Hudnut hails. As such, we know there's a case-of-the-week format, and we know that a network show isn't necessarily beholden to the production values of, say, an HBO drama. But is there any rule that states the show has to be made with the dimmest possible audience members in mind?

"Marshals" keeps reiterating the plot of each episode in the simplest terms possible, with the latest example coming in "Secret Weapon." After the team finds tire tracks near the barn where Rudy Carpenter died, it becomes clear that someone other than Carpenter is transporting missing bombs elsewhere. Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) then announces, "Someone's driving this bomb around right now and we got no idea what the target is." Is this like the Netflix thing where they assume people are on their phones and aren't paying close enough attention?

These frequent consequence-free cliffhangers are another aspect of "Marshals" that gives the sense of a show doing an impression of a better show. It's like the writers know cliffhangers can be compelling, but don't want to cause any actual distress to an audience they evidently assume is made up of phone-addicted simpletons barely following the plot. So, we get these half-baked moments of tension, after which nothing changes. Remember when "Marshals" Season 1 introduced a powerful Dutton family rival who'd apparently been at odds with Kayce's family for generations, only for that same rival to be arrested several episodes later, never to be heard from again? It's the same thing. A threat arises, then it's neutralized. I get that "Marshals" isn't "Yellowstone." But does that mean it has to be bad?

#3507. Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Most Hated Dungeon Gets Reworked in Remake

Nintendo knows how you feel about the Water Temple

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is rightly praised as one of the best games ever made, but that exalted status has always come with a caveat: the Water Temple stinks. It seems that the people working on Ocarina of Time’s imminent remake are very much aware of this.

In an interview as part of Nintendo’s “Ask the Developer” series, longtime Zelda producer and developer Eiji Aonuma was asked whether the remake’s dungeons would change — for context, Aonuma designed these areas in the original game.

“I had some overdue homework: I wanted to do something about the Water Temple I created 28 years ago,” Aonuma said, then laughed. “Since it became well known for its difficulty in the original game, I had the team make some adjustments in this version.”

For those unaware, the Water Temple is infamous for combining slow underwater movement with confusing area layouts, resulting in a slog. You have to constantly pause and open menus to put on and take off a pair of Iron Boots that let you sink in water, making it even easier to get disoriented.

Aonuma explained why he wanted to build this area in the first place. “When I designed the Water Temple all those years ago, I wanted to create an experience where simply being underwater was fun," he said. "It was a time when there were very few 3D games that even let players go underwater. I enjoy freediving, and what I find fascinating about being underwater is how different everything feels. The sounds change, and it feels like you’re in a completely different space. I wanted to create a place where players could experience those sensations.”

“However, with the dungeon’s complex structure and a lot of item toggling involved, you often had to open the menu screen repeatedly, making it hard to keep track of where you were and which way you were facing,” he said, acknowledging the area’s flaws. “We addressed those issues in this version.”

“In this version, we’ve made item toggling much easier,” game director HokWai Ng added. Instead of navigating menus, the remake lets players quickly swap items with the d-pad. “We also changed some of the walls that made it easy to lose your sense of direction to lattice-style structures, making it possible to see the rooms beyond them and get a better sense of the overall space.”

The developers said they hope that the remake sparks conversations between young and older players about their experiences with Ocarina of Time. “You know, your Dad got stuck in the Water Temple plenty of times back in the day,” Ng said as an example. Aonuma responded, “Then kids playing this version might say, ‘Come on, it’s not that hard.’ Poor old Dad might end up feeling deflated.”

Early hands-on previews of the remake have been quite positive, and we won’t have to wait long to see how the final version lands, Water Temple 2.0 included. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is out on Nov. 5, exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2.

#3506. Liam Neeson's New 2026 Action Movie Flopped At The Box Office

Another year, another Liam Neeson action movie. What else is new? This time, it's a police chase flick in the form of "The Mongoose." Ever since "Taken" became a box office hit that led to Neeson's unexpected action star makeover, the Oscar-nominated actor has been churning these pieces of genre fare out with regularity. His latest effort, however, failed to drum up much business.

"The Mongoose" opened to just $464,421 on 1,014 screens over the weekend, making for a terrible $458 per-screen average. It was duking it out with the badly reviewed horror comedy "Christmas at the Kringles," which bombed with just $710,526 on just over 1,800 screens. Because Halloween fell on a Saturday, it was a lousy weekend for new releases, so Samuel Goldwyn Films decided to throw this one at the wall to see if it would stick. It didn't.

Directed by Mark Vanselow, Neeson's new actioner centers on Ryan "Fang" Flanagan (Neeson), a man who, having been accused of a crime he didn't commit, leads law enforcement on a cross-country car chase with the help of his brothers in arms, all while the public roots for his getaway. The film's cast also includes Marissa Tomei ("Spider-Man: No Way Home"), Ving Rhames ("Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning"), and Michael Chiklis ("The Shield").

This is actually Leeson's second action flick to come and go while hardly registering with the moviegoing public this fall, as "The Fix" also opened in theaters in September, making roughly $1.2 million domestically in total. The days of the "Taken" trilogy are indeed very far behind us, it seems.

Like many of Liam Neeson's late career action movies, "The Mongoose" isn't exactly a critical darling, having only earned a 30% approval rating among critics on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. That being said, this one was undoubtedly financed with the understanding that if it can be made at a certain price point, it'll find its audience on VOD/streaming.

Case in point, Neeson's "Blacklight" somewhat inexplicably took over Prime Video's streaming charts earlier this year, despite being considered one of the actor's worst films in recent memory. Similarly, in late 2024, Netflix breathed new life into Neeson's 2015 crime thriller "Run All Night." This sort of thing happens pretty regularly. People really enjoy these movies, even if it's more about enjoying them from the comfort of home. They may not be cinematic events, but they're good library titles that generate streaming revenue.

It's honestly been some time since one of Neeson's action movies was an out-and-out hit. 2018's "The Commuter" was like "Non-Stop" on a train and pulled in $120 million at the global box office. Ever since then, though, his films have tended to perform more like "The Mongoose." Setting aside the Neeson vehicles that were hampered by the pandemic, "The Marksman," "Blacklight," "Memory," "Marlowe," "Retribution," and "Absolution" are all real movies, yet each of them either disappointed or outright flopped at the box office.

We're arguably far removed from Neeson's best action movie "The Grey" or hidden gems like "A Walk Among the Tombstones." His recent efforts have tended to follow a very basic formula, and while it may not sell tickets in theaters, it clearly makes money elsewhere within the Hollywood ecosystem.

#3505. Star Trek's Gates McFadden And John De Lancie React To Death Of Patrick Stewart

It's never easy saying goodbye to heroes we grew up adoring, but some deaths take even longer than others to process. The loss of "Star Trek" and "X-Men" legend Patrick Stewart still doesn't feel quite real yet, even as it feels like we've spent every day since celebrating all of his greatest and most memorable moments on the screen. When it comes to the tight-knit bonds formed between members of the "Trek" family, well, they've proven that it really is a family. Some relationships have experienced more friction than others, such as the widely-publicized rift between William Shatner and the late Walter Koenig, but others have gone through the fire and emerged stronger than ever.

That sense of history through the decades is probably why two celebrations of Stewart's life hit harder than the rest. In a pair of separate posts, "Star Trek: The Next Generation" co-stars Gates McFadden and John de Lancie both memorialized their longtime friend and screen partner. Cast as Beverly Crusher and the enigmatic cosmic being Q, respectively, McFadden and de Lancie represent two of Jean-Luc Picard's most popular and well-established character dynamics throughout their collective run on "Trek." Both shared countless memories together with Stewart on- and off-screen, and, fittingly enough, both received satisfying send-offs alongside their captain on "Star Trek: Picard."

For those prone to bursting into tears over such heartbreaking tributes, be warned that this will likely unleash the waterworks.

Jean-Luc Picard meant so much to so many, and Patrick Stewart's portrayal of the venerated captain represented something deeper and more meaningful than a simple "Trek" character. And while fans all over the world have attempted to verbalize just how important he was, the woman behind Dr. Beverly Crusher has now captured it as eloquently as only she can.

Gates McFadden was one of the many Hollywood icons who initially reacted to Stewart's passing. But in a guest article in Variety, she's penned a full-length eulogy for her friend's well-lived life. However, though it's well worth reading in full, one particular passage draws a direct link between the integrity of Stewart's performance as Picard and our desperate need for genuine leadership in real life (a particularly poignant message on the U.S.' Election Day):

"One thing is for certain: Patrick's reach across the continents was massive. After word of his death surfaced, the internet, not surprisingly, was filled with thousands of tributes of admiration and overflowing love for the Yorkshire man. He touched so many people in so many ways. Not only was he the captain of the Enterprise crew, he seems to have been everyone's captain because of how he walked in the world.

What a breath of fresh air to have a leader who cared about the ethics of what he said! The result was eloquence. Seriousness. Intellect. The character of Jean-Luc Picard, which Patrick played brilliantly, was the antithesis of many of our leaders today."

McFadden sums up Stewart's life and his tragic loss thusly: "Jean-Luc Picard embodied that ideal. Patrick's death means the loss of Picard, which for some hurts even more than the loss of Patrick Stewart. Jean-Luc gave us hope."

Where Dr. Beverly Crusher brought both a platonic and romantic dimension to her relationship with Jean-Luc Picard, Q represents a very different extreme of emotions. Picard's longtime frenemy spent many an episode of "The Next Generation" annoying our good captain to no end, oftentimes outwitting our hero and proving himself an equal match in intellect or philosophy. But their two diametrically opposite perspectives on humanity added so much to their adventures over the years and, ultimately, reached a tearjerking crescendo in the Season 2 finale of "Star Trek: Picard" as they say an emotional goodbye to one another.

Actor John de Lancie struck that exact same tone in a Facebook post over the weekend. It's not easy to encapsulate such a complicated, prickly, but oh-so-entertaining dynamic between two such worthy opponents, but the Q scene-stealer certainly found a way. In a much shorter (though no less sincere) remembrance, he stated:

"For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard's side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn.

Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him.

The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing.

We couldn't have said it any better than that. Most Trekkies would put the Q and Picard rivalry up there among the best in the entire franchise — a testament to Stewart and de Lancie's easy chemistry and witty repartee. It's devastating to know we'll never see that on-screen again, yet reassuring to know it'll always stand the test of time.

Will Captain Jack Sparrow suit up for one last ride? At the very least, Johnny Depp isn't ruling it out, but the actor has a condition to return for "Pirates of the Caribbean 6." Depp is in the midst of mounting a Hollywood comeback following his fall from grace several years ago, thanks to his highly publicized legal feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard. The Depp/Heard case was even explored in a two-part Discovery+ documentary. Now, though? He's back and may (emphasis on "may") yet return to his most famous role.

During a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight for his Hollywood comeback movie "Ebenezer," the actor was asked about reprising his role as Jack Sparrow in the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" film, which has been in the works at Disney for some time. Here's what he had to say about it:

"If things are exactly where they need to be with regard to how they are going to top off the 'Pirates' franchise ...The only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.

At another point, it was suggested that the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" movie would be a total reboot. Multiple scripts have been developed, yet nothing has stuck. Basically, this movie is going to happen at some point, with or without Depp. So, Disney needs to decide what, exactly, it wants to do here. We'll see how it all shakes out.

#3503. Daniel Craig's Early-Career Miniseries Is A Masterpiece Every British TV Fan Has To Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When I saw a 24-year-old Daniel Craig play the sadistic South African Police Sergeant Jaapie Botha in John G. Avildsen's 1940s Apartheid drama "The Power of One," I can't say that I had him pegged for the next James Bond, but I did know that he was a remarkably hissable villain. The film quickly faded from memory, but every time Craig turned up in a movie during the 1990s, I'd remember how effective he was as Botha, and wonder why he wasn't getting meatier roles.

What I didn't know at the time was that he'd given a tour de force performance in the 1996 BBC drama serial "Our Friends in the North." The nine-part series spans 31 years in the lives of four friends from Newcastle upon Tyne, and boosted the careers of Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston and Gina McKee. But no one demonstrated greater range than Craig, whose character, Geordie, flees an abusive, alcoholic father to pursue an unpromising life in low-level crime.

British television wasn't immediately accessible in the United States in 1996 (unless it was a pop cultural sensation like "The Office" or "Little Britain"), so I didn't find out about "Our Friends in the North" until a decade later, directly after Daniel Craig had rejuvenated the James Bond franchise in "Casino Royale." I can understand why it didn't leap over the pond. The historical references are specific and steeped in British politics, which, to American viewers, makes it somewhat daunting. But Peter Flannery's writing and the dynamite acting ensemble will hook you just as sharply as David Simon plunged you into the Baltimore social stratum with "The Wire."

Unfortunately, "Our Friends in the North" isn't readily available in the United States on streaming, but if you've got a region-free Blu-ray player you can purchase it for $33.00 on Amazon, and it's worth it. I grew up watching British crime movies like "The Long Good Friday," "Mona Lisa," and "The Krays," and Flannery's writing doesn't suffer fools. But his dialogue is so crisp and layered and immaculately performed that you feel compelled to understand it. You're thrust into a society that, from the corrupt parliament down to the alcoholic, homeless dregs, is foreign yet familiar.

Craig's Geordie faces the most dire swings of fortune. He's not a bad person, but, like so many people who choose a criminal lifestyle and succumb to substance abuse, he makes so many compromises that there's eventually no way out. It's a harrowing journey and I wish I could tell you it ends well for Geordie, but "Our Friends in the North" is not out to comfort.

#3500. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

Tragically, Crichton couldn't produce more shows after ER, as he passed away at age66 in 2008. Still, Crichton's legacy lives on through popular shows inspired by his iconic works.

Nearly a decade after his death, HBO adapted Crichton’s 1973 cult classic film Westworld into a TV show, which lasted four seasons. The dystopian Western series revolves around a technologically advanced amusement park, where wealthy guests fulfill their Wild West fantasies with the help of human-like android robots called “hosts.” However, things go terribly wrong when the hosts start acting outside their programming and gaining autonomy. When the show debuted in 2016, Westworld became an instant global phenomenon, with critics and audiences praising its stellar ensemble cast, masterclass storytelling, high production quality, and timely, thought-provoking themes.

While Westworld remains one of HBO's most intriguing and ambitious shows ever, it isn't the best Crichton TV series. That title belongs to Netflix's animated series Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous, which is set at the same time as Chris Pratt's 2015 blockbuster film Jurassic World. Premiering in 2020, Camp Cretaceous follows six teen campers working together to survive after being left behind on Isla Nublar during the dinosaur outbreak. The sci-fi adventure show ended its five-season run with an average rating of 92% on Rotten Tomatoes, surpassing the entire Jurassic Park and Jurassic World franchises.

There are many reasons why Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous is absolutely the better Crichton series than Westworld. In terms of narrative structure and consistency, the Netflix show stayed true to the franchise's central themes and plot while keeping the kid-centric storyline fresh and exciting. Even though Westworld earned acclaim for its masterful season 1, it failed to live up to expectations as the seasons progressed because its storytelling became incoherent.

The creative team, led by creators Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy, went overboard trying to make Westworld more mysterious and twisty, which ultimately shifted the show away from its core themes. This alienated the audience with overcomplicated storylines and contributed to the HBO series' declining viewership and ratings.

Another reason why Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous has surpassed Westworld is its well-planned character development, which made the show's ending more worthwhile. Throughout Camp Cretaceous' run, Darius (Paul-Mikél Williams), Brooklynn (Jenna Ortega), Ben (Sean Giambrone), Kenji (Ryan Potter), Sammy (Raini Rodriguez), and Yaz (Kausar Mohammed), who are collectively called the "Nublar Six," remained as the show's emotional anchor. Their unwavering loyalty and unlikely friendship were what drew fans to become invested in their journey.

As for Westworld, although it introduced strong, compelling characters like Dolores (Evan Rachel Wood), Bernard (Jeffrey Wright), and Maeve (Thandiwe Newton), their development took unexpected turns that made it harder for the audience to stay connected to their stories.

HBO's 4-part sci-fi thriller series was canceled a season too soon, but it has now returned as a digital hit right before a reboot is set to happen.

Because the show changed so much during its final two seasons, Westworld didn't get the chance to wrap up its story properly. Shortly after its season 4 finale in 2022, the series was canceled due to its plummeting viewership, permanently ending Westworld on a cliffhanger. Unlike the HBO sci-fi show, Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous delivered a satisfying conclusion by staying true to the core theme of Crichton's original Jurassic Park story. No major narrative mysteries went unanswered, and all the main characters got complete story arcs.

Although Universal Pictures’ Jurassic World movies were blockbuster hits, Netflix’s Camp Cretaceous is the superior Jurassic Park sequel. Critics and fans alike praised the animated series for returning to the franchise’s roots by flawlessly capturing the survival tone and horror vibe of Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park novel, which many of the live-action films lacked. While Colin Trevorrow’s blockbuster franchise shifted its focus to delivering elaborate action sequences, Camp Cretaceous was more grounded and focused onthe characters’ vulnerability against unpredictable, genetically engineered prehistoric animals.

Camp Cretaceous not only featured more of the iconic Isla Nublar, introducing new sides of the terrifying island, but also showcased different perspectives on Jurassic World’s dinosaur outbreak, even taking the audience to the aftermath of the 2015 movie. This aspect was overlooked in the live-action adaptation, as the Jurassic World franchise moved on to a much broader global scale.

#3498. 5 Best Movies Like The Love Hypothesis

There was never any doubt that Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" would become a big hit for Prime Video. Streaming platforms have struck gold by taking romance books and turning them into comforting crowd-pleasers for the small screen. Sometimes this results in films as vapid as "My Fault: London," but often it results in charming movies that take allow us to indulge romantic fantasies via two hot people falling in love.

That's exactly what we got when "The Love Hypothesis" transformed from "Star Wars" fan fiction, of all things, into a novel and then a streaming movie. Ali Hazelwood's book about a biology PhD student who pretends to date her professor, only for the two to fall deeply in love became a hit, and was promptly given a film adaptation in which Reinhart plays the student, Olive Smith, while British actor Tom Bateman plays the ornery professor, Dr. Adam Carlsen.

There were two main tropes to both the book and the film: mismatched lovers who cross a boundary to be together, and the good old fake relationship that becomes very real. Of course, this is far from the first time these tropes have been used in romance movies, which is why it's actually quite easy to recommend films just like "The Love Hypothesis." While there are plenty of golden-age romance movies that used these plot devices (1941's "Come Live with Me" saw James Stewart and Hedy Lamarr fake a marriage only to fall head over heels), we're betting that fans of Reinhart's movie will want more modern examples. With that in mind, here's a list of the best movies like "The Love Hypothesis."

"My Oxford Year" may have a controversial ending but it's got everything you could want from a modern-day streaming flick based on a book. Melodrama and fairytale romance combine in this Netflix movie, which stars Sofia Carson (who's fast becoming the streamer's go-to romantic drama leading lady) as American exchange student Anna De La Vega. Before descending into a life of corporate drudgery, Anna decides to study Victorian poetry at the University of Oxford for a year. Wouldn't you know it, once there she meets an unreasonably charming and handsome English DPhil student and tutor named Jamie Davenport (Corey Mylchreest).

"My Oxford Year" shares much in common with "The Love Hypothesis." Not only are both based on books (though the former actually began as a screenplay before it was adapted into a novel), they both feature a student/teacher relationship that gets off to a rough start only to flourish into a modern-day fairytale. Both also feature strapping English leading men (though Bateman plays an American in "The Love Hypothesis") who start out as jerks only to reveal a tender side as things progress.

It is worth noting that there's a tragic element to "My Oxford Year," so if you're looking for something that wraps up as neatly as "The Love Hypothesis," this might not be the ideal watch. But otherwise fans of Lily Reinhart's movie should fall madly in love with Carson's alternative.

These streaming movies are all well and good but there has to be at least one undisputed classic on this list. There's no better example of the fake relationship trope than this 1990 romantic comedy in which we got to see prime-era Richard Gere and Julia Roberts fall for one another. The movie did what "The Love Hypothesis" and its fellow streaming-age rom-coms did decades before Netflix was even a thing, bringing together impossibly beautiful stars via a fake relationship that blossoms into the real thing.

If you don't know the plot of what might just be Julia Roberts' best movie, I'm not sure what to tell ya. He's a corporate raider, she's a sex worker he asks for directions. So begins a love affair that sees Gere's Edward Lewis paying Roberts' Vivian Ward to spend a week with him and act as his girlfriend. Needless to say, this confected relationship becomes a real one. Ward melts Lewis' cold corporate heart and Lewis draws out the real Ward from behind a wall of dissociation built up over her time spent as a sex worker.

If you're somehow yet to see the film, and are worried the tale of a millionaire corporate raider falling for a sex worker might not have the wholesome charm of "The Love Hypothesis," don't worry. There's a reason Roger Ebert called the film "the sweetest and most openhearted love fable since 'The Princess Bride.'" "Pretty Woman" is as romantic a comedy as they come. But beyond that, it somehow manages to feel grounded thanks to its multi dimensional characters, without compromising the fairytale romance aspect.

Sofia Carson will soon have a monopoly on streaming romance movies. Her 2025 romantic drama "The Life List" dominated Netflix just prior to the similarly successful release of "My Oxford Year." But before either of these movies, Carson made her Netflix romance debut with the 2022 film "Purple Hearts." Guess what — the whole thing was based on a book, Tess Wakefield's 2017 novel of the same name.

In "Purple Hearts" we get a modern day version of James Stewart's "Come Live with Me." This Carson-led love story sees the former Disney Channel star play diabetic waitress and musician Cassie Salazar, who's working herself ragged just to afford insulin. Her salvation arrives in the form of hunky Marine Luke Morrow (Nicholas Galitzine), who agrees to marry Cassie so she can gain health coverage and he can benefit from a pay bump. You can see where this is going.

Much like with "The Love Hypothesis," this is a story about a couple who agree to act as though they're together only to develop real feelings along the way. There's plenty of BookTok-style melodrama on display here, too, which should please anyone who enjoyed the tension of the third act fall-out in "The Love Hypothesis."

It's the film that made Glen Powell a star and proved Sydney Sweeney could make popular stuff outside of "Euphoria." If your favorite thing about "The Love Hypothesis" was watching two attractive people make out, then "Anyone But You" should be right up your alley. In fact, "Anyone But You" is arguably the apotheosis of the modern day two-hot-actors-fall-in-love rom-com. But there's a stronger connection between this film and "The Love Hypothesis."

Lily Reinhart's Olive Smith and Tom Bateman's Dr. Adam Carlsen agreed to fake a relationship for mutually beneficial reasons, and the same happens with Sweeney's Beatrice Messina and Powell's Ben. The duo pretend to be a couple so that Bea's parents will stop trying to repair her relationship with her ex, and Ben can make his own ex jealous. We all knew where it was going from the very beginning but that didn't make it any less enjoyable to watch.

Unlike with "The Love Hypothesis," the guy in this romantic comedy isn't a complete jerk. Full of himself, maybe, but not an anti-social hermit like Bateman's "Dr. Evil." Still, he and Sweeney's law student don't exactly get along, especially after their first meeting ended on awkward terms. That, alongside the fake relationship trope, gives Powell and Sweeney's couple a similar dynamic to that of Olive and Adam in "The Love Hypothesis." So if you somehow missed the unlikely box office smash that was "Anyone But You" back in 2024, now's the time to remedy that.

In 2018, "To All the Boys I've Loved Before" became the new gold standard for teen rom-coms. It also happens to be a nice little companion to "The Love Hypothesis." Based on a book? Check. Fake relationship trope? Check. Academic setting? Sort of check. Rather than college, this tale of teen love, adapted from Jenny Han's YA novel, plays out in high school, where Lara Jean Covey (Lana Condor) writes secret letters to her crushes. Of course, she never intends for any of them to read her missives, but guess what — that's exactly what happens.

Lara Jean's biggest crush is Josh Sanderson (Israel Broussard), and when she sees him approaching with his letter in hand, she kisses another one of the letter recipients, Peter Kavinsky (Noah Centineo) in an attempt to throw Josh off. Soon, Peter and Lara Jean are fake dating. This allows the former to distract from the embarrassment of Josh receiving a letter, and the latter to make his ex-girlfriend Gen (Emilija Baranac) jealous. But you know how this goes. Real romance develops, melodrama ensues, feelings get hurt.

"To All the Boys I've Loved Before" is, however, more than your standard BookTook phenomenon turned Netflix romance movie. The film is surprisingly well shot, retains a heartfelt sensibility throughout, and isn't afraid to embrace its classic fake relationship rom-com influences. It's a touching little high school melodrama that's well worth a watch for anyone who even remotely enjoyed "The Love Hypothesis."

BREAKING RULES WITH OTHER MOMMY: Cast and filmmakers discuss subverting horror tropes through Bela's perspective and disrupting the expected cadence of the genre.

#3494. TV Legend Ed Asner Appeared In This Classic '60s John Wayne Western

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In 1966, John Wayne visited Vietnam and began formulating one of his biggest on-screen blunders, "The Green Berets." Before he could get around to making the one John Wayne film that Roger Ebert called "cruel and dishonest," however, he had another couple Westerns to get through. "El Dorado" was the first. It premiered in the United States in June 1967, exactly one year after Wayne made the rounds in IndoChina. At the time, the Duke was becoming increasingly irrelevant as the Western genre began its shift into the revisionist age. Nonetheless, "El Dorado," which saw Wayne reunited with his frequent directorial collaborator Howard Hawks, became a success. It also remains the only film to feature Wayne and Ed Asner, who at the time was just three years away from debuting in his best-known role as Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show."

Asner began acting in the mid-1950s. He made his TV debut in 1957 on "Studio One" and his film debut in 1962, appearing alongside Elvis Presley in "Kid Galahad." Oddly enough, he didn't appear in a Western film until 1966 when he joined Wayne in "El Dorado," which considering any working actor of the 1960s was bound to wind up in a Western at some point is surprising.

Asner did, however, appear in some classic Western TV shows, guesting on "Outlaws" in 1962 and "The Virginian" the following year. He also appeared in two episodes of "Gunsmoke" and in 1965 joined Robert Horton for a single installment of "A Man Called Shenandoah." When he set foot on the "El Dorado" set, then, while he hadn't yet appeared in a big screen Western, he was well acquainted with Hollywood's vision of the Old West. Now all he had to do was face down John Wayne.

"El Dorado" is directed and produced by Howard Hawks. His frequent collaborator Leigh Brackett wrote the script, which she considered to be her finest work. In Todd McCarthy's "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," Brackett is quoted as having said, "I wrote the best script I have ever written and Howard liked it, the studio liked it, Wayne liked it, and I was delighted." Unfortunately for her, Hawks wanted to play things a little safer by essentially remaking "Rio Bravo," the 1959 John Wayne-led Western that launched an unofficial trilogy.

"Rio Bravo" was the result of Hawks and Wayne's hatred for "High Noon," which featured a sheriff too scared to confront the antagonists alone. Hawks and Wayne's retort featured a more muscular hero who had no problem facing evil solo. It proved so successful and seemingly suited Hawks' sensibility so well he essentially remade it twice, once with "El Dorado" and again with 1970's "Rio Lobo" — both of which starred the Duke. The former was a more lighthearted movie, however, with James Caan as John Wayne's sidekick providing much of the comic relief due to his poor aim.

Otherwise, "El Dorado" starred Robert Mitchum, the film noir legend who was also no stranger to the Western, as the alcoholic sheriff of the titular town, J.P. Harrah. His old pal, gunfighter Cole Thornton (Wayne), arrives in El Dorado after being been hired by local tycoon Bart Jason (Ed Asner) to drive the poor MacDonald family off their land so he can claim it for himself. After talking to Harrah, however, Thornton refuses Jason's offer, and things don't exactly go smoothly.

Ed Asner — who passed away in 2021 at the age of 91 — played the villain of "El Dorado." It must have been intimidating for the early-career Asner, then in his mid-30s, to have to square up to John Wayne. "I found myself going into uncharted territory," he told Jake's Takes in 2021. "I regarded myself as a big liberal. I hadn't been proved yet as a liberal, but a big liberal, and here I was going against one of the biggest reactionaries of the times. I didn't know how I'd be treated." According to Asner he was "roasted on the first day" but "passed the roast test" and ultimately found the Duke to be "a nice reasonable fellow."

It probably helped that "El Dorado" was a success. Roger Ebert called it "the most entertaining Western to turn up this year" and according to "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," the film did "outstanding business" following its 1966 debut in Japan. It then went on to generate "rentals of $6 million on box office receipts of $12 million," which ultimately made it the 12th biggest picture of 1967. Not bad for Asner's first big screen Western.

Ironically, considering his initial collaboration with Wayne was so amiable, the very series that made Asner a star, "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," came to represent a form of TV entertainment that heralded the end of the TV Western as a result of the "rural purge." Not that Wayne himself was affected, but the more urban-focused TV slate of the 1970s was one major signifier that the world was moving on from the days when Wayne and his fellow Western heroes proudly rode the plains.

In the TTRPG, this powerful magic item in D&D lets the creature attuned to it sprout a pair of golden wings from its back.

This gives the creature a Fly Speed of 80 feet, and any creature that tries to make an Opportunity Attack against it when they fly out of range has Disadvantage on the attack roll. Another great thing that Aviana’s Feather does is reduce the fall rate to 60 feet per round until you land, much like Feather Fall, one of the best reaction spells in Dungeons and Dragons.

The Goblin Jumper Cables are one of the most surprising magic items in the World of Warcraft expansion, and you wouldn’t actually guess that from its name. This Uncommon Wondrous Item lets you use a Magic action to attach the cables to a dead creature and try to bring it back to life.

You’ll need to succeed on a DC 15 Arcana check with Tinker’s Tools to bring a dead creature to 1 Hit Point, if they died during the last minute, and not of old age. If you fail the check, you take 2d6 Lightning damage. This item can’t be used again until the next dawn. Effectively speaking, Goblin Jumper Cables are a free Revivify every day – it’s not a guaranteed revive, but tons of tables, like Critical Role, already add a check to Revivify anyway.

I’m a big fan of teleportation skills in any game, and the Hearthstone is one of my favorites from the new D&D: World of Warcraft release. The Uncommon Wondrous Item lets you take a Magic item to set a place, like an inn, as the destination for your item’s teleportation. Then, you can activate it with a Magic action and 1 minute of prepping to teleport directly to the set destination.

It works very much like the Hearthstone in the MMORPG, and it’s a great way of touching base in any campaign, even if it only teleports one character. It’s particularly useful if your party doesn’t have easy access to teleportation spells. Imagine you need to get a quick warning to the king after discovering evidence of a plot against him inside a dungeon? A Hearthstone can save his life (and get you rewards for doing so).

The Judgment Armor is the piece of gear every Paladin or heavy-armor Cleric in Dungeons and Dragons has ever dreamed of. Judgment Armor is a Legendary Plate Armor that will work with anyone proficient in Heavy Armor, but it’s made for those attuned to the divine.

When wearing this armor, the creature is under the effects of the Detect Evil and Good and Protection from Evil and Good spells. This happens with no Concentration and entirely for free. On top of that, if you are a Paladin, you can extend the effects of Protection from Evil and Good to creatures of your choice in your Aura of Protection.

Using a charge system like many different magic items in D&D, the Life-Staff of the Web Lair is an arguably broken choice for anyone. While attuned to this Legendary staff, the creature basically has access to Spider Climb and can ignore restrictions caused by webs. On top of that, you know the location of any creature in contact with the same web as you.

Of course, you can cast Web for free with it. If a creature is in contact with your Web, you can use another charge to force a DC 18 Constitution save, and if they fail, they take 4d10 Necrotic damage or half as much if they succeed. Regardless of that, you regain Hit Points equal to half of the damage dealt. This new World of Warcraft magic item turns battlefield control into an HP-draining feast.

Straight from the inventory of Sprinkle Noggenfogger in World of Warcraft, the Noggenfogger Elixir in D&D is just like it is in the MMORPG. This Rare potion can be consumed for three different random effects. Once you drink the Noggenfogger Elixir, you roll 1d6.

On a 1-2, you take a skeletal form for 1d4 hours, and you don’t need to breathe for that duration. On a 3-4, you gain the Reduce effect of the Enlarge/Reduce spell for 1d4 hours, without the need for Concentration. On a 5-6, your rate of descent while falling slows to 60 feet per round for 10 minutes, like an extended Feather Fall. If you’re planning any type of heist or prison break, the Noggenfogger Elixir may come in handy.

The Potion of Mana may be one of the most unbelievable magic items added to D&D with the new World of Warcraft expansion. Alternative ways of recovering spell slots are rare in the TTRPG. Although there are items like Pearl of Power and some class features like Arcane Recovery or Magical Cunning, once you’re out of spell slots, you need to rest.

The Potion of Mana comes in different rarities, but effectively, it lets you recover a spell slot. The Common version lets you recover a Level 1 spell slot, while the Greater (Uncommon) lets you recover a Level 1-3 spell slot. The Superior (Rare) version restores a Level 1-5 spell slot. Warlocks have never rejoiced so loudly.

If you think the Potion of Mana is good, the Potion of Rejuvenation will blow your socks off. Like the previous item, its rarity varies depending on how good it is. The thing with the Potion of Rejuvenation is that it not only restores a spell slot, but it also restores Hit Points for the creature who drinks it.

The regular (Uncommon) version of it restores 3d4+3 HP and a Level 1 spell slot, while the Greater version restores 6d4+6 HP and a Level 1-3 spell slot. The Superior Potion of Rejuvenation restores 9d4+9 HP and a Level 1-5 spell slot. This new magic item is so good it’s pretty broken if you think about it.

There are tons of magic weapons in D&D: World of Warcraft, like the iconic Ashbringer and Frostmourne, but most of them are extremely powerful and feel like weapons above tier 4 play. Shalamayne, however, feels like a proper tier 4 weapon to wield. This Artifact item is a +3 Greatsword that deals an extra 2d12 Force damage on a hit.

It also enables Graze and Sap to be triggered simultaneously, in addition to becoming two +3 Longswords, Shalla’tor and Ellemayne. Shalamayne is a proper high-level weapon that you can easily see a hero of Azeroth wielding to take down the Lich King from World of Warcraft.

Vithrak, Gaze of the Deadman is a very fun new magic item to wield. This Very Rare Ring has a limited number of charges per day, and with it, you can expend a charge to learn all the Resistances, Vulnerabilities, and Immunities of a creature you can see within 120 feet of yourself.

Mind you, there are other features in the TTRPG that grant similar effects, much like the Extract Aspects feature from the Way of the Cobalt Soul Monk subclass, but this one works with any creature. It’s perfect if you’re planning a surprise attack on enemies or if you’re in a rough spot during a fight. There are several other remarkable magic items in the World of Warcraft expansion for Dungeons and Dragons, but these stand out immensely.

When IndieWire’s Kate Erbland reviewed the film out of TIFF, she singled out Coon’s rich performance as a clear high point of the film.

#3487. The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece. Related Stories To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies in Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3485. Patrick Stewart’s Most Terrifying Role Officially Surges on Streaming

Some actors become so synonymous with one or two roles that it's easy to forget that they're immensely talented performers, and when you've spent decades commanding the Enterprise or guiding the X-Men as Professor Charles Xavier, audiences probably aren't expecting you to suddenly become one of the most terrifying villains in modern horror. Yet that's precisely what Patrick Stewart did ten years ago as he gave audiences one of the most unpleasant performances in recent memory. Audiences are now rediscovering it.

Stewart's brutal R-rated horror thriller Green Room has officially climbed into the Top 4 of America's streaming movie rankings, reaching No. 3 on JustWatch's U.S. chart. After witnessing a crime, a rock band is unexpectedly thrust into a life-or-death battle to escape from a diabolical club owner and his henchmen.

The fllm stars Anton Yelchin (Star Trek) as Pat, Imogen Poots (28 Weeks Later) as Amber, Patrick Stewart (X-Men) as Darcy Banker, Alia Shawkat (Arrested Development) as Sam, Joe Cole (Peaky Blinders) as Reece, Callum Turner (Masters of the Air) as Tiger, Macon Blair (Blue Ruin) as Gabe, and Mark Webber (Scott Pilgrim vs. the World) as Daniel. The movie is directed by Jeremy Saulnier (Blue Ruin).

Your instincts, your strengths, and your particular way of thinking under pressure point to one villain you actually have a fighting chance against. Everyone else — good luck.

Jason is relentless, but he is also predictable — and that is the gap you would exploit.

Michael watches before he moves. He is patient, methodical, and almost impossible to detect — until it's too late for anyone who isn't paying close enough attention.

Freddy wins by getting inside your head — using your own fears, your own memories, your own subconscious as weapons against you. That strategy requires a target who can be destabilised.

Pennywise is ancient, shapeshifting, and feeds on terror — but it has one critical vulnerability: it cannot function against someone who genuinely stops being afraid of it.

Chucky's greatest advantage is that nobody takes him seriously until it's already too late. He exploits the gap between how something looks and what it actually is.

Green Room earned widespread acclaim upon its release, particularly for Saulnier's relentless direction, its realistic depiction of violence, and Stewart's deeply unsettling performance as the calculating leader of a white supremacist organization.

The film holds a 90% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, with reviewers praising its atmosphere, performances, and refusal to soften its extraordinarily grim subject matter. As for the violence, there’s certainly no shortage of blood and carnage. There’s shotguns, boxcutters, attack dogs and so much more. Green Room features some of the most impressive gore and makeup effects work you're likely to see in a while and Saulnier revels in his achievement, taking the time to let his camera linger on the gruesome details.

Its renewed streaming popularity offers another opportunity for audiences to discover one of the most intense horror thrillers of the past decade, and it's a great window into Stewart's ability as an actor for those who only know him from Star Trek and X-Men.

Green Room is currently available to stream in the United States, including on Netflix.

#3483. All 16 Episodes Of Netflix’s Teen Psychological Thriller Are Leaving In 2 Days

Netflix's critically acclaimed 16-part series The End of the F***ing World officially leaves the platform on November 5, 2026, meaning the last day to watch it on the platform is on Wednesday, November 4. The psychological drama/dark comedy series is one of Netflix's top-rated original series of all time, earning a 94% Rotten Tomatoes score and a similarly strong 92% RT audience score. For these reasons and more, The End of the F***ing World is worth watching from start to finish before it's removed from Netflix later this week.

The End of the F***ing World subverts that traditional coming-of-age road trip series on its head with its mature themes, complex characters, and dark sense of humor. The series was nominated for two Emmy Awards, both in cinematography categories, and is based on a popular graphic novel of the same name by Charles S. Forsman. The End of the F***ing World was developed for television by Charlie Covell (Kaos) and stars Alex Lawther (Alien: Earth) and Jessica Barden (Dune: Prophecy) as two outcasts who become unlikely friends. What begins as a genuine search for an estranged family member becomes a journey of violent crime across England.

Lawther plays James in The End of the F***ing World, a seventeen-year-old who believes he is a psychopath and meets Alyssa (Barden), a rebellious teen who wants to run away from home. James has been acting on his violent tendencies throughout his adolescence by killing small animals and convinces himself that it's time that he kills a human being. When Alyssa gives him an ideal opportunity to make his first kill on a road trip in the remote suburbs of England, James begins plotting her death, only to discover that he may have a heart after all, or at the very least a genuine connection with Alyssa.

While the overall premise of The End of the F***ing World sounds quite morbid, viewers and critics alike enjoy the series for its sharp black comedy and psychological elements. The Hollywood Reporter writes, "The twisted, efficient story that The End of the F***ing World tells is a nicely contained thing that requires no additional embellishment and it should be binged and cherished in its tart glory." Similarly, The Guardian notes, "It's fabulous - comedy so dark that you can barely make out the comedy. And yet it is funny, as well as being convincing."

Netflix’s new police procedural offers 59 episodes of twisting investigations, compelling characters, and one of network TV’s best crime mysteries.

If you enjoy other hidden-gem dark comedy series like Wayne and I Am Not Okay With This, then The End of the F***ing World is the perfect binge for you on Netflix this week. The series is one of several that are leaving Netflix in the near future due to an expired 7-year licensing deal with Channel 4, one of the most popular TV networks in the UK, and there is no clear indication at this time of when or if the series will be returning to Netflix anytime soon. The End of the F***ing World is simply one of the best coming-of-age series with dark comedy and psychological thriller elements that has ever been on Netflix, so don't miss your last chance to binge it this week.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
